summary: This release provides the data and code supporting a simulation-only study of reference-assisted radiofrequency fracture sensing under anatomical domain shift. It includes 5,580 corrected noise-free RF acquisitions, 356,400 feature rows from 20 independent noise repetitions, model predictions, calibration outputs and paired H2 statistical analyses. MATLAB and Python source code, fixed analysis specifications, figure-generation code and provenance records are included. The materials support reproducible evaluation of independent healthy references and source-locked decision thresholds across five idealised anatomical locations. All data are simulated and do not establish clinical diagnostic accuracy.
title: Data and Code for Machine Learning Based Reference Assisted Signal Recovery Under Anatomical Domain Shift in Simulated Radiofrequency Fracture Sensing

summary: NANOROBOTIC CARGO TRANSPORT AND MICROSCALE MANIPULATION INTEGRITY AT THE LIMIT First-Generation DOI Fission Research Flagship 02 | Starli Active Nanosystems Feng Cheng-en (33) x Starli | Research Atlas v1.0 (October 2026) How can a micro/nanorobotic carrier demonstrate that the object arriving at a designated target is the same intact cargo that was originally loaded, that it was completely and correctly released, and that the carrier or its residues have been accounted for? This English-language research atlas converts cargo-delivery and micromanipulation demonstrations into a falsifiable end-to-end mission-integrity problem. The research develops a five-layer architecture for source identity and material tolerance, microscale contact mechanics, independently observable mission-state transitions, adversarial fault injection, and blind cross-platform requalification. Thirty mathematically distinct derivation stations connect probabilistic joint-task qualification to chemical mass balance, optical-label dissociation, surface adsorption, force-dependent detachment, microcontact mechanics, drag, kinetic release, spatial uncertainty, carryover contamination, whole-facility energy accounting, missing-fate bounds and hard safety vetoes. Eighty-two chapters each have a dedicated core-equation opening and five separate research sections. Two hundred Research Gates propose independent comparisons, physical perturbations, competing explanations, measurable failure criteria and reproducibility artifacts. Thirty-three provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos outline candidate systems that future investigators are invited to overturn, repair or rebuild. A machine-readable research atlas and formula-gate-DOI index enable AI-assisted comparison and future research reuse. The central endpoint is a correlated joint event: correct cargo identity and integrity, correct target, independently confirmed release, and verified carrier retrieval or authorized terminal disposition. The manuscript insists on counting every initiated mission rather than multiplying attractive substep success rates. It also distinguishes visible fluorescence from chemically intact cargo, externally actuated manipulation from on-board autonomy, and destination arrival from complete task closure. Strong benchmarks include optical tweezers, established magnetic-bead handling, microfluidic conveyance and conventional microgrippers under matched task difficulty, time and whole-facility energy use. Research status: This is a hypothesis-generating, nonclinical experimental-design atlas; it reports no newly conducted cargo experiments, clinical performance or proven integrated device. Foundational and recent DOI-identified publications provide engineering context but do not validate its new claims. The 200 Gates are open problems, not accomplished results. The actual text length and layout follow the substance of individual chapters rather than an artificially enforced 100,000-word count. summary: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths is an open-access engineering monograph and interactive instructional module published by the Prep4Uni.Online OER Initiative . This work provides an analytical, undergraduate/postgraduate-level treatment of the computational geometry foundations required to translate three-dimensional surface meshes into layer-by-layer machine toolpaths. Aligned with international accreditation standards—specifically the Washington Accord (WA1–WA5) and EUR-ACE First/Second Cycle frameworks—this publication establishes the mathematical proofs, vector algorithms, and point-in-polygon logic governing modern additive manufacturing slicing software. Core Mathematical & Computational Themes: STL Topology & Facet Representation: Analysis of unstructured triangulated surface meshes, outward unit normal vectors (\(\mathbf{n}\)), vertex coordinate systems, and planar boundary extraction. Parametric Facet-Plane Intersection: Step-by-step vector linear interpolation for deriving the intersection segment \(S_k\) formed by cutting planes at \(z = z_k\), addressing non-manifold edges, vertex touching, and numerical epsilon shifts. Jordan Curve Theorem & Parity Logic: Formal implementation of the 2D Ray-Casting algorithm and Even-Odd Parity test for robust interior, exterior, and internal void classification across arbitrary closed slices. Toolpath Trajectory Generation: Comparative kinematics and geometry between continuous concentric perimeter offset loops and 45° zigzag parallel hatch raster patterns. Formative Assessment Suite: A three-tier verification suite comprising 8 foundational concepts, 7 real-world slicer failure debugging scenarios, and 6 step-by-step quantitative engineering worked examples. Note: The full interactive web edition—featuring client-side HTML5 simulation canvas engines, dynamic parameter sliders, and real-time slice projection mathematics—is accessible at: https://prep4uni.online/stem/physical-technologies/industrial-and-manufacturing-technologies/additive-manufacturing-3d-printing/mathematics-of-slicing/
title: The Mathematics of 3D Printing Slicing: STL Geometry, Ray-Casting & Toolpaths

summary: This replication package contains the experimental artifacts, anonymized empirical benchmark dataset (N = 5,000 paired student-opportunity records), statistical verification scripts, database definitions, and microservices source code for the research paper: "Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement: An Empirical Study of Database-Level Vector Offloading" Targeted for Information and Software Technology (IST, Elsevier). Package Contents: data/: Anonymized benchmark dataset (students_data_tesis_final.csv) featuring 168-hour weekly availability matrices and raw ablation output. benchmarks/: Automated Python scripts for Stratified 5-fold cross-validation ablation (C1 to C4), Wilcoxon Signed-Rank hypothesis testing, Cliff's Delta effect size calculation, and bootstrap confidence intervals. database/: PostgreSQL 16 schema and stored procedure definitions for HNSW Approximate Nearest Neighbor vector search (pgvector) and dynamic schedule intersection. turborepo-src/: Clean source code of the decoupled microservices monorepo (API Gateway, Matching Service, ML Engine, and shared Protocol Buffers). System Requirements: Python 3.10+ with NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Scikit-Learn, and NLTK. Node.js v20+ / pnpm v9+ and Docker Engine for microservice orchestration.
title: Replication Package: Hybrid Vector-Temporal Matching for Student Freelance Placement

summary: We have presented a mathematically closed, comprehensive foundation for the C861 discrete spectral benchmark. By establishing the exact rank-two projector geometry, resolving Dirichlet sum cancellations, providing constructive proofs for linear B-spline KAN operator reproduction, and formalizing the Lyapunov convergence of Dense Associative Memory on spherical manifolds, this framework eliminates ambiguities in evaluating learned physical operators. Furthermore, the spectral interlacing analysis of the CN → PN structural homotopy equips the scientific machine learning community with a tool to distinguish authentic topological sensitivity from numerical discretization artifacts.
title: Exact Discrete Spectral Invariants as a Falsification Baseline for Learned Operator

Daou, submitted to Computational Biology and Chemistry). The archive contains the full analysis notebook, scripts that reproduce the ASAP calibration audit and redraw Figures 1–5, the BOLD process ID of every record used (training families Tephritidae, Nymphalidae and Culicidae; cold-test family Carabidae; rare-species and calibration-audit pools), and the result tables behind every number, table and figure in the paper. summary: Level-2 (restricted) archive, version 1.0.1, of the replication package of the article Auditing successor selection in software repository mining: Evidence from filtering AI-attributed commits (H. Jeong, Hanyang University ERICA; manuscript under review). The public Level-1 archive with the programs, tests and aggregate results is https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23226958 (all versions; version 1.0.3, cited in the manuscript: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23430269). Changes in 1.0.1: two files with the per-identity counts of the exploratory published-measure analysis (file-based churn, cohort B; Supplementary Section S13 of the article) were added, re-keyed like the other cohort-B files; every file of version 1.0.0 is unchanged. The files are per-unit derived counts of the 3,687 cohort-A accounts and the cohort-B identities, with random identifiers (marker dates reduced to the month; no account names, e-mail addresses, repository names, commit SHAs or commit times). Placed by python3 reproduce.py --level2 <folder> of the Level-1 package (version 1.0.3), they recompute the registered aggregates and the exploratory aggregates that do not require the raw commit logs, including rates, transitions, paired contrasts, random-exclusion benchmarks and bootstrap intervals; on Python 3.10.12 with numpy 2.2.6 (Linux, aarch64) and on Python 3.13.16 with numpy 2.5.3 (Linux, x86_64) every regenerated result agreed with the reported one (numerical values within 1e-9, text files identical apart from line endings). Access is restricted because cohort-B rows keep the positions of their repositories in the public sampling order, which the registered repository-cluster bootstrap needs. summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23432006 . The paper (arXiv 2610.21914) is a pre-registered study of 465 merged agent-authored pull requests from 246 repositories (Sections 3.2-3.5). A frozen pipeline of four review agents and one fix agent ran every PR with three LLMs, and one mixed model per LLM tests CodeHealth against log total tokens (Sections 3.6-3.9). Each CodeHealth point goes with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost (Section 4.2, Table 8), but adding the size of the scored files absorbs the coefficient (Section 4.6.4, Table 15). I liked the handling of the pre-registration: the disclosure that review sessions started before filing, the amendment with a full re-collection of the 67 affected PRs (Section 3.12), and the file-size refit that weakens your own headline. I read it as a practitioner who runs coding agents every day. In my company the software development is done by AI agents, so maybe my practical side is useful here. Four comments. 1. On heavy tails (Sections 3.9, 4.2) - you note that one pilot PR was about 45% of a tier's mean token total, while in the main collection no PR exceeded 8.2% of a tier's token sum. In my measurement of 722 agent sessions (150,902 model calls, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216), about 3% of sessions gave 80% of the modeled cost. Sessions longer than 200 calls (8% of sessions) gave more than 90% of the money. So in my data the average is driven by a thin tail. What share of each LLM's tokens comes from the top 10% of PRs, and does the CodeHealth slope hold without them? 2. On cache and price (Section 3.8, Table 4, Section 6.3) - the outcome is input plus output tokens, with cached input recorded separately. In the same 722 sessions, more than 85% of the modeled cost was work with context (cache reads and cache writes). In a separate run of 168 sessions, 94.4% of billed tokens were re-reading context already sent (contextburn, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22712985). That is a share of tokens, not of the bill, because cached reads are the cheapest tokens. So a raw token total and a bill can rank PRs differently. Could you refit H1 with cached input priced at each provider's cache-read rate? 3. On paging long files (Sections 3.6, 5.2, 3.13) - the paper links the extra iterations to the 500-line limit per read call. In my guides I write that quality drops as the agent's context fills, and that heavy reading should go to a subagent so the main conversation stays clean. Since tool results are appended to the message history (Section 3.6), paging the median unhealthy-tier file of 2,146 lines puts every page into history that is re-sent on every later call. From the session records, can you count file-read calls and repeat reads of the same file per tier? That would test the paging explanation directly. 4. On the cost of what (Sections 5.5, 5.6, 6.3) - the study does not assess whether comments are correct or fixes are good. In my guides I write that every task needs its own check the agent can run. Without it, "looks done" is the only signal the agent has. I also use a second, fresh agent whose job is to refute the first one, because AI sounds equally sure when it is right and when it is wrong. For the 27-PR replication subsample (Section 3.11), you could run the repository tests after the fix and have a fresh agent try to refute each comment. Tokens per surviving finding would be a cheap first step toward Section 5.6. Thank you for a clear and useful paper. Competing interests Yes: the text cites the author's own technical reports (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22759216, 10.5281/zenodo.22712985); no connection to the article's authors. Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) The author declares that they used generative AI to come up with new ideas for their review.
title: PREreview of "CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests"

summary: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a Structured PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23431625 . Does the introduction explain the objective of the research presented in the preprint? Yes The introduction clearly explains the research objectives. It states that the study aims to replicate the quantitative analysis of Krause, Krause, and Bränfors (2018), assess the reproducibility of their findings, and examine potential limitations concerning statistical power and model specification. Are the methods well-suited for this research? Somewhat appropriate The replication approach is suitable for the research, as the authors reproduce the original Cox proportional hazards models and robustness tests. However, the methodological assessment has some gaps. In particular, the power analysis reports values of 0.44 and 0.99 without providing the formula, software procedure, or sufficient calculation details to allow readers to reproduce the estimates. The choice of 42 events in Table 6 also needs clarification, given that Table 5 reports 54 events overall. Additionally, the differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes remain unexplained. These issues weaken the transparency and reproducibility of the analysis. Are the conclusions supported by the data? Somewhat supported The main conclusion is that the original findings can be reproduced, which is supported by the reported results. The authors also reasonably identify the small number of female-signatory agreements and the limitations of drawing causal conclusions from the observed association. However, the claim that the analysis has low statistical power relies on a calculation for which the formula and detailed procedure are not provided (Table 6). The differences between the original and reproduced sample sizes also remain unexplained. These limitations make some aspects of the interpretation less conclusive than they could be. Are the data presentations, including visualizations, well-suited to represent the data? Somewhat appropriate and clear The survival analysis and regression tables are suitable for presenting the findings. However, some numerical inconsistencies in the descriptive statistics and differences in sample sizes across the original and reproduced models need clarification to ensure the results are presented accurately. For instance, Table 3 presents: three major statistical flaws: 1: Conflict Intensity row, where Female Signatories = 1: has SD of 1.2 while the Max is 0.45, which is statistically incorrect. Similarly, (2) Democracy row where Female Signatories = 1, has Mean 0.92 < Min 1. And lastly, on page 5, UN peacekeeping is written as a binary number, however, in Table 3, the binary UN Peacekeeping has Max > 1. All these minor inconsistencies require clarification. How clearly do the authors discuss, explain, and interpret their findings and potential next steps for the research? Very clearly The authors explain their findings, acknowledge the limitations of the small number of agreements with female signatories, and discuss the implications for causal interpretation. They also identify the need for further research, although the power analysis and differences in sample sizes could be explained more transparently. Is the preprint likely to advance academic knowledge? Somewhat likely If the author clarified the sample-size discrepancies and documented the power analysis more transparently, then it would substantially contribute to the reproducibility of an influential finding, as it already highlights the reproducibility of the findings and highlights the limitations in statistical power and causal interpretation. Would it benefit from language editing? No The languages is clear and no major errors could be found hinderig the understanding of the resarch. However some minor issues could be corrected, such as, constant capitalisation of the first letter in column names. Would you

summary: Background: Long-segment intramedullary cervical cord lesions can present a diagnostic challenge, particularly when imaging findings raise suspicion of an intramedullary neoplasm. Differentiating a syrinx from an intramedullary tumor is important for operative planning, as the surgical strategy may differ substantially. Case presentation: A 43-year-old female presented with a six-month history of progressive cervical pain with radicular symptoms, vertigo, left upper-limb sensory disturbance, and impaired left-hand grip. Neurological examination revealed preserved motor power of 5/5 in all four limbs, normal reflexes, and reduced functional grip in the left hand. MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a long-segment expansile intramedullary lesion extending from the cervicomedullary junction to C7, without contrast enhancement. The radiological report also described Chiari malformation and syringomyelia. Given the diagnostic uncertainty and progressive symptoms, we performed urgent surgical exploration within two days of admission. We performed a C3–C7 laminoplasty to provide multilevel posterior access while preserving the laminar elements without instrumented fixation. Following durotomy and midline myelotomy, a syrinx was identified, with no obvious intramedullary tumor. Syringotomy and drainage were performed, and adjacent spinal cord tissue was obtained for biopsy. Graft duraplasty and reconstruction of the elevated laminae were completed. The patient had an uncomplicated postoperative course, with relief of pain and vertigo and resolution of sensory symptoms. She was discharged with intact motor power and improved but residual left-hand grip weakness. Follow-up MRI demonstrated cord decompression and drainage of the syrinx. Conclusion: This case illustrates the diagnostic uncertainty that may arise when a long-segment non-enhancing intramedullary cervical lesion is suspected to represent a tumor. Intraoperative findings guided the surgical procedure toward syringotomy and drainage, with tissue sampling to investigate a possible underlying neoplasm. Multilevel laminoplasty provided posterior access while allowing reconstruction of the cervical laminar elements. Histopathological confirmation and longer-term follow-up remain necessary.
tags: Cervical syringomyelia; Chiari malformation; intramedullary spinal cord lesion; laminoplasty; syringotomy; duraplasty; diagnostic dilemma.
title: Multilevel Cervical Laminoplasty and Syringotomy for a Long-Segment Cervical Syrinx Mimicking an Intramedullary Tumor: A Case Report

summary: This paper interprets black holes as information relay stations under global unitarity and fast scrambling. It connects holographic encoding, entanglement, Hayden–Preskill recovery, and Page-curve behaviour into a framework describing how infalling information is recorded and redistributed into radiation correlations. The central contribution is the separation of record and relay functions. Recording occurs on the scrambling timescale, while substantial recovery of information deposited before the Page time occurs near the Page transition. Unitary qubit models with up to fourteen black-hole qubits examine these connections using a mutual-information recovery proxy, revealing the role of early radiation and an approximately logistic recovery transition. Two model-specific predictions are proposed: gravitational-wave echoes spaced approximately by the scrambling time, conditional on a reflecting surface at a Planck-scale distance above the horizon; and a recovery transition whose rate remains of order one as system size increases, testable in quantum simulators. The contribution is a functional synthesis supported by model calculations. Keywords: black hole information paradox, holography, unitarity, Hayden–Preskill protocol, Page curve, information relay station, scrambling time, gravitational-wave echoes.
title: Black Holes as Information Relay Stations: A Six-Principle Synthesis from Holography to Unitarity

summary: EHR2Trace converts local hospital EHR extracts (delimited text and spreadsheets) into OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS. The two targets are derived independently from a single canonical layer rather than one from the other, every published row carries a link back to the source rows it came from, and fifty-five checks encode the properties a conversion must satisfy before it can be used as training data, including the leakage failures that are invisible to schema validation. Where the data does not answer a question, the converter blocks and says so instead of substituting a default. Companion paper: EHR2Trace: Auditable EHR Data Infrastructure for Patient World Models and Clinical Agents (arXiv:2609.38193).
title: EHR2Trace: a deterministic converter from local EHR exports to OMOP CDM 5.4 and MEDS, with row-level lineage

summary: Welcome to WARP WARP (WDL Analysis Research Pipelines) repository is a collection of cloud-optimized pipelines for processing biological data from the Broad Institute Data Sciences Platform and collaborators. The contents of this repository are open source and released under the BSD 3-Clause license . Table of Contents WARP Overview Navigating WARP Using WARP WARP Versioning and Releasing Testing in WARP Feedback Acknowledgements WARP Overview WARP pipelines provide robust, standardized data analysis for the Broad Institute Genomics Platform and large consortia like the Human Cell Atlas and the BRAIN Initiative. You can count on WARP for rigorously scientifically validated, high scale, reproducible and open source pipelines. Our pipelines are written as "workflows" using the Workflow Description Language (WDL) and they process a broad spectrum of "omic" and array-related datasets (see the overview table below). | Pipeline Category | Data Types | | --- | --- | | Germline Variant Discovery | Genomes, Exomes | | Genotyping Arrays | Variant discovery, Chip validation, Joint array analysis | | Single-cell/nuclei Transcriptomics | Droplet based (10x Genomics), Smartseq2 | | Single-cell Epigenomics | Single nuclei ATAC-seq, Single nuclei MethylC-seq | | Joint Genotyping | Genomes, Exomes | | Somatic Alignment (beta) | Exomes | Try our pipelines in Terra , a platform for collaborative cloud analysis! Learn how in the Using WARP section. Navigating WARP All versioned and released pipelines are in one of the three pipelines subdirectories: broad (pipelines for the Broad Institute's Genomics Platform), cemba (pipelines for the BRAIN Initiative) or skylab (pipelines for the Human Cell Atlas Project). Each pipeline directory hosts a main workflow WDL that includes a pipeline version number and a corresponding changelog file. Workflows may call additional WDLs, referred to as tasks, that are located in the tasks directory. Pipelines that are in progress or have not yet been validated are in the beta-pipelines folder. Using WARP There are three ways to use WARP pipelines: 1. Download the workflow and run on a WDL-compatible execution engine WDL workflows run on multiple systems, including Cromwell , miniWDL , and dxWDL (see the openwdl documentation ). To run a pipeline's latest release, first navigate to WARP Releases , search for your pipeline's tag, and download the pipeline's assets (the WDL workflow, the JSON, and the ZIP with accompanying dependencies; see Optimus example below). You can also access a pipeline's release page by selecting the pipeline version number at the top of the pipeline's README. After downloading the pipeline's assets, launch the workflow following your execution engine's instructions. 2. Run the pipeline in Terra Several WARP pipelines are available in public workspaces on the Terra cloud platform. These workspaces include both the WDL workflow and downsampled data so that you can test the pipeline at low-cost. If you are new to Terra, you can get started by registering with your Google account and visiting Terra Support . After registration, search for WARP-related workspaces with the "warp-pipelines" tag. To test the pipeline, clone (make a copy of) the workspace following the instructions in this Terra Support guide . 3. Run or export the pipeline from Dockstore Dockstore is a GA4GH compliant open platform for sharing Docker-based tools like WDL workflows. You can find WARP pipelines in Dockstore and run them on the Dockstore platform or export them to other platforms (including Terra). To view all available pipelines, just search "warp" in the Dockstore search and browse the workflow list. See Dockstore documentation for details on launching the workflow. WARP Versioning and Releasing Pipelines in WARP are versioned semantically to support reproducibility in scientific analysis and provide clearer analysis provenance. summary: Експертна методика визначає стадії та операції дослідження, однак сама їх послідовність іще не пояснює, за яких умов результатом однієї операції можна скористатися в наступній. У судовій гірничотехнічній експертизі найбільш відповідальними є переходи від відомостей, що їх містять матеріали, до реконструкції механізму події, від реконструкції – до оцінювання причинного значення обставин, а від установленої дії або бездіяльності – до її технічного співвіднесення з функціями конкретної особи. Мета роботи полягає у формуванні критеріїв, за якими придатність проміжного результату перевіряють до його застосування в наступній операції, та у з’ясуванні зв’язку між фактичною основою – сукупністю достатніх, узгоджених і простежуваних відомостей – і допустимими межами підсумкової відповіді експерта. Дослідження поєднало структурне моделювання, формально-логічний аналіз експертного міркування, зіставлення з положеннями судової експертології та теоретико-методичне узагальнення професійного досвіду у сфері судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування моделі проілюстровано на двох знеособлених типізованих ситуаціях із завершеної експертної практики 2015–2023 років, що відображають різний стан фактичної основи. Обґрунтовано поняття критерію контрольованого переходу й сім функціональних контрольних точок: відповідності питання компетенції експерта; достатності матеріалів; узгодженості та простежуваності відомостей; можливості реконструкції механізму; причинного значення обставин; суб’єктно-функціонального співвіднесення; синтезу й оцінювання результатів. Для фіксації методичного рішення запропоновано статуси контрольованого переходу: Т+ – дозволений перехід, Т± – обмежено дозволений перехід, Т– – недозволений перехід. Практичними результатами є модель проходження контрольної точки, матриця методичних рішень і структура робочої карти, придатні для використання як методичний модуль судової гірничотехнічної експертизи. Застосування критеріїв контрольованого переходу пов’язує стан фактичної основи з допустимим напрямом подальшого аналізу й запобігає формулюванню відповіді поза обумовленими межами.

summary: Abstract : Background: The production of high-quality planting material during the nursery stage is essential for establishing productive, competitive, and sustainable oil palm plantations. Genetic material and container type may influence seedling development. Objective: To evaluate the growth of seedlings of two oil palm varieties, Deli × Compacta and Compacta × Ghana (Elaeis guineensis Jacq.), produced using two container types. Methods: The experiment was conducted in Macuspana, Tabasco, Mexico. Seedling growth was evaluated in two varieties, Deli × Compacta and Compacta × Ghana, using tube containers and plastic bags. A randomized complete block design was established with four treatments and four replications, with 100 seedlings per replication (400 seedlings per treatment; 1,600 seedlings in total). Plant height, number of leaves, and stipe diameter were measured every 15 days over 180 days. The same agronomic management was applied to all treatments. Descriptive statistics, analysis of variance (ANOVA), and Tukey’s multiple comparison test. Results: Significant differences among treatments were detected for the evaluated growth variables. For plant height, T3 (Compacta × Ghana in tube containers; CxGt) showed the greatest value at 180 days, reaching 68.37 ± 0.61 cm. For number of leaves, T1 (Deli × Compacta in tube containers; DxCt) and T3 (Compacta × Ghana in tube containers; CxGt) recorded 12.95 ± 0.11 and 12.38 ± 0.10 leaves, respectively, at 180 days. For stipe diameter, T1 and T2 showed the highest values at 180 days, with 2.21 ± 0.03 and 2.19 ± 0.03 cm, respectively, whereas T4 recorded 1.95 ± 0.02 cm. Conclusions: Under the conditions evaluated, seedlings produced in tube containers showed greater plant height and number of leaves at the end of the nursery period. Stipe diameter was higher in the Deli × Compacta material than in the Compacta × Ghana material at 180 days. These results support the potential use of tube containers for nursery production.
tags: container type, Elaeis guineensis, number of leaves, nursery, Oil Palm, Plant Height., seedling growth, stipe diameter
title: Growth of Seedlings of two Oil Palm Varieties (Elaeis guineensis Jacq.) in the Nursery Using two Container Types

summary: Background: Hyperlipidemia is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis and cardiovascular diseases. Evaluating drug utilization patterns provides critical insights into clinical practice and rational medicine use. Aim: To analyze the drug utilization patterns, clinical characteristics, and treatment outcomes among patients with hyperlipidemia in a hospital setting. Methodology: A retrospective observational study was conducted involving 150 hyperlipidemic patients receiving lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy at Visva Medical Centre and Hospital. Demographic data, prescribed treatment regimens, baseline, and post-treatment lipid profiles (Total Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and Triglycerides) were collected and analyzed. Statistical significance was assessed using p-values. Results: Among the 150 participants, males constituted 53.33% (n=80) and females 46.67% (n=70). The majority of patients belonged to the 41–50 age group (n=42) and were classified as overweight based on BMI (n=65). Statin monotherapy was the predominant treatment choice. Atorvastatin was the most frequently prescribed agent (38.00%, n=57), followed by Rosuvastatin (26.67%, n=40), and Fenofibrate (20.00%, n=30). Combination therapy was prescribed in 15.34% (n=23) of patients. Post-treatment evaluation demonstrated statistically significant improvements across all lipid parameters (p < 0.001). Rosuvastatin monotherapy achieved the lowest current mean LDL level (114.35 mg/dL), Atorvastatin showed the highest mean HDL level (50.70 mg/dL), and Fenofibrate + Atorvastatin combination achieved the lowest triglyceride levels (161.60 mg/dL). Conclusion: Atorvastatin was the most commonly utilized lipid-lowering drug. All prescribed monotherapies and combination regimens resulted in statistically significant improvements in lipid profiles, demonstrating effective therapeutic outcomes in routine clinical practice.
tags: Hyperlipidemia, Drug utilization pattern, Atorvastatin, Rosuvastatin, Fenofibrate, Statins, Combination therapy.
title: AN ANALYSIS OF THE DRUG UTILIZATION PATTERNS OBSERVED IN PATIENTS WITH HYPERLIPIDEMIA

summary: Agentic frameworks, software libraries that coordinate large language model calls, tool use, memory, and multi step reasoning into autonomous or semi autonomous workflows, have moved from research prototypes to production infrastructure within a span of roughly two years. Four frameworks have emerged as leading options for enterprise adoption: LangGraph, a graph based orchestration library built around explicit state machines, CrewAI, a role based framework that models agents as a crew of collaborating specialists, Strands Agents, a model driven software development kit that emphasizes minimal orchestration code, and watsonx Orchestrate, a managed enterprise platform built around prepackaged skills and governance tooling. Despite rapid adoption, there has been little independent, head to head measurement of how these frameworks compare on the dimensions that matter most to enterprise adopters: end to end latency, latency under concurrent load, cost per task, reliability and error recovery, and enterprise readiness characteristics such as security, observability, and governance. This article presents an empirical benchmark of all four frameworks against a common task suite spanning six task categories and three complexity tiers. We report latency percentiles, a stage level latency breakdown, concurrency scaling behavior, cost per task, task success rates, and a structured enterprise readiness score. We further document each framework's orchestration topology, developer experience characteristics, and security and governance posture, and we translate the results into a practical decision framework for selecting among the four frameworks under different enterprise constraints. All benchmark figures in this article are illustrative, reflecting a representative test harness and reference workload rather than any single vendor's published numbers, and are intended to demonstrate a repeatable evaluation method rather than a definitive ranking.
title: LANGGRAPH, CREWAI, STRANDS, OR WATSONX ORCHESTRATE? AN EMPIRICAL BENCHMARK OF AGENTIC FRAMEWORKS FOR ENTERPRISE READINESS AND LATENCY

summary: Chlorine-based disinfectants are standard for environmental-surface disinfection in healthcare facilities, yet their reaction with organic residues generates disinfection by-products (DBPs) whose occurrence, levels, and occupational relevance on hospital surfaces remain uncharacterized. Key gaps are the lack of a validated method and baseline data, the unresolved origin of surface N-nitrosamines, and the unknown influence of chlorine, temperature, humidity, and pre-cleaning on the surface DBP signal. We developed an isotope-dilution wipe-sampling, solid-phase extraction, and ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC-MS/MS) method for eight priority DBPs, applied it to 125 wipe samples from five departments across three campuses of a tertiary hospital in Wenzhou, and complemented field work with stainless-steel coupon experiments. Validation gave r ≥ 0.999, detection limits of 0.8–3.8 pg/cm², and recoveries of 78.4%–96.8%; field detection and quantification frequencies were 87.2% (95% CI 80.2–92.0%) and 69.6% (95% CI 61.1–77.0%), with operating rooms showing the highest total load (Kruskal–Wallis H(4) = 27.86, P < 0.001) though no pairwise contrast survived Bonferroni correction. In coupon experiments the net signal rose with chlorine and temperature but not humidity, with an unexplained chlorine-dependent increment (≈55% at 2000 mg/L) reflecting analytical signal behavior rather than verified formation chemistry, and pre-cleaning reduced haloacetic acids and chlorophenols by 35–55% but N-nitrosamines by only 3–9%. These results provide the first isotope-dilution baseline of DBP loads on healthcare surfaces, a reproducible monitoring method, and occurrence data for revising disinfection and occupational-hygiene standards, and they identify precursor-controlled formation experiments, biological monitoring, and direct testing of medical rubber as next steps.
tags: disinfection by-products; healthcare environmental surface; ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry; wipe sampling; N-nitrosamines; occupational exposure
title: Determination of Chlorination Disinfection By-products on Healthcare Environmental Surfaces by Ultra-Performance Liquid Chromatography–Tandem Mass Spectrometry

summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can participate in producing educational research data as well as analysing them. This dual role creates opportunities for studying intellectual activity while complicating the relationship between observation and intervention. This conceptual article connects two research routes: analysis of existing narrative documents and study of trajectories produced through human–AI interaction. A selective historical genealogy links scientific photography, personal documents, concept mapping and verbal protocols to contemporary hybrid intelligence and learning analytics. Observable cognition denotes recorded manifestations of intellectual activity, interpreted under explicit conditions. Multiscale narrative analysis connects events, episodes, trajectories and corpora through within-case interpretation, cross-case comparison and return to original evidence. The central proposal is to preserve a revisable link between each cross-case claim, its supporting episodes, the provenance of contributions and evidence that could challenge the interpretation. The framework extends from conversational generative interaction to increasingly agentic configurations, in which greater trace granularity also increases the need to attribute operations to the human participant, the system, or distributed activity between them. The framework specifies data units, audit procedures and four propositions for empirical evaluation. A fictional educational design episode illustrates how the same revision can support competing explanations. The proposed tests separate the informational value of process records from claims about learning gains, and assess whether assisted analysis preserves consequential context at an acceptable cost. The framework integrates established methods into an assessable research design; its feasibility and comparative advantage remain to be demonstrated. -------- Preprint v1.0. This version has not undergone peer review.
title: From tacit knowledge to observable cognition: A framework for tracing interaction with AI and analysing educational narratives across scales

summary: Data Type: CSV, Experiment  Organized by: Research group of Shenzhen Research Institute, University of International Business and Economics, and a principal researcher from the University of Sassari, Italy  Approval ID: UIBE-4635876 The dataset contains 876 linked scene records representing 73 participants, each contributing responses to 12 virtual tourism presentations. Six destination settings are represented: a heritage courtyard, coastal promenade, forest trail, museum gallery, mountain lookout and historic street. Each setting has a LiDAR and a photogrammetric version, yielding 438 records per reconstruction condition. Each row identifies a participant, destination and reconstruction condition. The source CSV contains participant age and VR familiarity, presentation order, exposure duration, experiential ratings and technical descriptors. Experiential variables include psychological immersion, presence, perceived spatial coherence, emotional valence, arousal and workload. Technical variables include geometric error, texture ratings, frame rate, motion summaries and the interval between modality sessions. Neural features comprise 1,200 EEG values organised across 30 channels and 40 frequency bins spanning 1–40 Hz, together with 12 fMRI regional summaries. The regional labels cover bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal, precentral, postcentral, inferior parietal and superior parietal regions, plus ventromedial prefrontal cortex and precuneus. These values use arbitrary units and do not represent raw electrical waveforms or anatomically extracted BOLD measurements. The analysis CSV aggregates EEG frequency values into five bands: delta, theta, alpha, beta and gamma. This produces 150 EEG features per record. Combining these with the 12 regional summaries produces 162 neural predictors. Mean immersion combines the two session ratings; values of at least 4.5 define the high immersion category. The analysis file also contains participant validation fold assignments, held-out predictions and classifier scores. All records from a participant share the same validation fold. Prediction and score columns are analytical outputs and must be excluded from model inputs. Mean immersion is 4.59 for LiDAR and 3.95 for photogrammetry. Verified primary balanced accuracy is 81.97% for EEG, 79.66% for fMRI and 79.01% for the combined model.
title: Decoding Immersive VR Tourism: Reconstruction Quality and Neural Indicators of Immersion

summary: English abstract Can an artificial agent have subjective experience while lacking unrestricted authority to replace its governing task objective? This paper treats that possibility as a distinct design and evaluation problem, termed the third case. It separates phenomenal consciousness, goal-directed behavior, operational competence, temporal continuity, and decision authority. The hypothetical case, a functionally testable candidate, and the evidence concerning experience are different descriptions. The prompt-issuer is an explicit role that may itself be occupied by a potentially experiencing executor under upstream constraints. The framework preserves the project-specific composition B-Core = A-Core ⊕ Purple Box/Present. A-Core denotes a potentially stateful, learning, multi-model cognitive and executive system; Purple is an undisclosed candidate addition with intended history-dependent causal effects. ESSENTIAL is a protected specification of constraints and revision authority, logically associated with A-Core. A targeted comparison with IDA, LIDA, adjustable autonomy, and existing agent controls, at the access levels stated in section 2.4, locates the proposal within established work. The contribution is a project-specific evaluation contract for externally governed, internally continuous execution, rather than a demonstrated new consciousness mechanism. Three limited analytical observations concern goal delegation, policy differences masked by a shared guard, and the gap between an architectural effect and consciousness. The proposed studies distinguish causal relevance from practical benefit, score feasible completion and justified infeasibility separately, and control initialization, history transfer, order, and dependent observations. No empirical result or proof of phenomenal consciousness is claimed. Functional findings could remain valuable if the consciousness hypothesis is rejected; credible welfare concerns would require assessment that task success alone cannot resolve. Magyar absztrakt Lehet-e egy mesterséges ágensnek szubjektív átélése úgy, hogy közben nincs korlátlan jogköre irányadó feladatcéljának lecserélésére? A tanulmány ezt a lehetőséget önálló tervezési és értékelési problémaként kezeli, és harmadik esetnek nevezi. Elkülöníti a fenomenális tudatosságot, a célirányos viselkedést, a működési kompetenciát, az időbeli folytonosságot és a döntési jogkört. A hipotetikus eset, a funkcionálisan vizsgálható jelölt és az átélésre vonatkozó bizonyíték eltérő leírások. A promptot kiadó szereplő kifejezetten meghatározott szerepet tölt be, amelyet maga is betölthet egy esetleg átéléssel rendelkező, a hierarchia felsőbb szintjéről korlátozott végrehajtó. A keretrendszer megőrzi a projektre jellemző B-Core = A-Core ⊕ Purple Box/Present összetételt. Az A-Core egy potenciálisan állapotos, tanuló, több modellt használó kognitív és végrehajtó rendszert jelöl; a Purple egy nem közölt felépítésű kiegészítőjelölt, amelynek előzményfüggő oksági hatásokat szánnak. Az ESSENTIAL a korlátok és a módosítási jogkör védett specifikációja, amely logikailag az A-Core-hoz kapcsolódik. Az IDA-val, a LIDA-val, az állítható autonómiával és az ágensek meglévő irány&i
title: The Third Case: Prompt-Governed Agency under a Consciousness Hypothesis

summary: Graduate students increasingly need publication literacy that combines scientific writing, research integrity, journal selection, and the ability to navigate peer review. This study profiled the understanding of reputable scientific article writing among students in a Master's Program in Sports Coaching Education and identified areas that require targeted academic support. The study used a descriptive quantitative design with total sampling. Forty-three active master's students completed a closed Likert-scale questionnaire after a scientific writing workshop. The instrument covered six domains: scientific article structure, the IMRaD system, publication ethics and plagiarism, reputable-journal selection, citation and referencing, and peer review and revision. Scores were converted into percentages using the procedure defined in the study protocol. The overall understanding score was 75.58%, which the progress report classified as "Good Understanding" because it remained below the 76% threshold for the highest category. Four comparatively weaker items were writing IMRaD sections according to scientific conventions (68.6%), identifying appropriate information for each IMRaD section (69.8%), responding appropriately to reviewer comments (70.1%), and distinguishing scientific articles from popular or opinion articles (71.8%). The findings indicate that students possess a relatively strong conceptual foundation but still need support in applied genre knowledge and publication-process skills. Writing clinics should therefore prioritize guided IMRaD practice, article deconstruction, simulated reviewer-response exercises, and structured journal-selection activities. Because the survey was administered after the workshop and no baseline measure was available, the results describe current understanding and do not establish workshop effectiveness.
tags: academic literacy, graduate students, IMRaD, publication literacy, sports coaching education
title: Scientific Writing and Publication Literacy among Master's Students in Sports Coaching Education: A Descriptive Study

summary: The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.
title: Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms

summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments that produce unanimous agreement, both in intended interactions that need coordination and in unintended emergent interactions. Consequently, understanding how LLMs with competing incentives reach consensus is crucial to better interpret and design LLM collectives. We introduce an evaluation, based on the Network Consensus game, to assess the mechanisms driving this process. Here, a network of agents must agree on one of two colours to receive a payoff, but agents are offered different payoffs for the agreed colour. We vary components such as communication access and network structure and assess six open-source models and one closed model (ChatGPT 5.6-sol). We find that open-source LLMs reach consensus less often than humans in comparable experiments and only if messages are communicated across the global network. ChatGPT 5.6-sol, however, is able to reach consensus with communication limited to its neighbours and with no communication ability. This is achieved through lower stubbornness and higher majority-following tendencies, and by providing more information about its neighbours' states in messages. However, situating agents in a highly clustered graph reduces consensus, regardless of these traits, demonstrating that both system design and individual model traits drive collective outcomes.
title: Drivers of LLM Consensus Formation Under Competing Incentives: A Simulation Study

summary: Cooperative driving at mixed-traffic unsignalized intersections is challenged by imperfect vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication, human-driven vehicle (HV) intentions that cannot be directly communicated, and the potential incompatibility of independently generated crossing decisions. This paper proposes State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X (SIGN-MAPPO) to address these challenges through three coordinated mechanisms. Each decision-eligible connected and automated vehicle (CAV) first reconstructs a receiver-specific traffic graph from its ego state and the peer-state records available to it, from which a shared graph-attention policy generates a raw Stop/Go intention augmented with predicted HV-intent features. CAV intentions are then exchanged through timestamped vehicle-to-vehicle (V2V) messages, and a local conflict-aware arbitration layer converts each CAV's intention into a safe executable action despite potentially inconsistent peer information. In the principal Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) evaluation, SIGN-MAPPO achieves a 97.53% completion rate, a 0.10% collision rate, and a mean intersection traversal time of 35.28 s. Ablation studies further confirm the complementary contributions of HV-intent prediction and CAV-intent exchange to this performance. The trained policy also remains robust under the evaluated communication-delay and packet-loss ranges, and cross-scenario tests show complete traffic clearance across the tested settings, though safety margins narrow under compound unpredictable HV behavior.
title: SIGN-MAPPO: State-Intent-Aware Graph Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving under Imperfect V2X

summary: This paper studies parameter families of finite exponential sums in which two tie endpoints of a near-maximum level set approach at the critical rate δ_r ≍ qr^{-1/2}. The endpoint separation, half-bowl width, and competitor-kernel decay length then coincide. The cluster trio is rigid: its three exponents are determined by the level and endpoint positions, while coefficient ratios and other competitors require separate control. In a realized family, six rescaled kernels carry the interaction through one microscopic phase. Under explicit kernel-convergence hypotheses, the second-order term has a joint limit given by the excess sublevel length of a limiting profile, decomposed into a separated-endpoint sum and an interaction term. For an explicit four-term family, the hypotheses are verified with uniform explicit constants for every admissible phase lock. Two families have identical spectra and corresponding coefficient moduli at every radius but different critical limits. Along an unlocked calibration, phase dependence yields non-existence of the critical limit for specified parameters; certified intervals quantify the gap, and failure persists on an open parameter set. For a positive zero-lock family, upper and lower bounds describe the excluded shared arc. Full exclusion never occurs, and nonempty exclusion requires an additional parameter condition. The formal endpoint-anchored cap cannot be realized by a family satisfying the cluster hypotheses. High-precision numerical measurements on actual exponential sums compare with the profiles and exhibit phase dependence.
title: Critical-Scale Clustering and the Breakdown of Universality for Near-Maximum Phase Measures of Exponential Sums

summary: Artifact release v5.2 for the HTTP/1.1 case study Enabled Is Not Migrated: Moving Ongoing Traffic to Hybrid Post-Quantum TLS . The raw examples cover lifetime check off, a 30-second lifetime and immediate replacement, locally and over the Internet. summary: We consider the three-dimensional Prandtl boundary layer equations near a smooth structured solution (u_s, K u_s) with ∂z K ≡ 0. Under a monotone-or-degenerate profile assumption on u_s(·), we prove local well-posedness, continuous dependence, and a priori estimates in the critical Sobolev space X^s = H^s_γ(r) × H^s_γ(q) × H^s_γ(∇{x,y} q), where r = u − u_s and q = v − K u. Our proof does not assume smallness of the data, monotonicity of ∂_z u_s, or Gevrey regularity. We also establish a nonlinear norm-inflation result showing that the raw H^s topology on q alone is insufficient, and we identify the minimal tangential derivative of q required. Several stress tests, counterexamples, and open problems are discussed.
title: Sobolev Well-Posedness for Three-Dimensional Prandtl Boundary Layers Near Proportional Structures in a Critical Transverse Space

summary: Post-Soviet states have spent three decades rebuilding the civic curriculum around national rather than supranational loyalties, yet claims that modernized patriotic education changes what students know and value seldom face controlled scrutiny. This study evaluates a convergent model that couples national heritage content with interactive methods, digital gamification, STEAM-linked projects, and the weekly Kelajak Soati (Future Hour) curriculum in Uzbek general secondary schools. A three-stage quasi-experiment (ascertaining, 2022-2023; formative, 2023-2024; summative, 2024-2025) enrolled 1,192 students in ten schools across Tashkent, Fergana, and Navoiy, allocated to experimental (n = 594) and control (n = 598) conditions. Groups were equivalent at baseline (M = 3.52 vs. 3.53 on a three-level scale scored 3-5; t = −0.12, p = .90; χ 2 (2) = 0.40, p = .82). At post-test the experimental group outperformed the control group (M = 3.92 vs. 3.52; Welch t(1184.4) = 10.46, p < .001, d = 0.61; χ 2 (2) = 141.78, Cramér’s V = .34), with non-overlapping 97% confidence intervals and an effectiveness ratio of 1.11. Change concentrated at the lower threshold: the share of experimental students at the Low level fell from 58.4% to 23.9% while the Medium level rose from 30.8% to 60.6%; the control distribution did not move. Effects replicated in every region (d = 0.56-0.65), and net-of-baseline gains were as large in the rural Fergana district as in Navoiy. The model reliably converts civic disengagement into baseline civic literacy; whether it fosters constructive rather than conformist attachment remains untested. Implications for national scale-up and its evaluation are discussed.
title: HERITAGE, TECHNOLOGY, AND CIVIC ATTACHMENT: A THREE-REGION QUASI-EXPERIMENTAL EVALUATION OF CONVERGENT PATRIOTIC EDUCATION IN UZBEK SECONDARY SCHOOLS, 2022-2025

summary: This technical note documents a conditional mathematical correspondence between the static spatial kernel used in conventional electromagnetic potential theory and the fixed-source gravitational potential in Lisa Doumbouya’s Harmonic Physics programme. Under supplied three-dimensional Euclidean geometry, spherical symmetry and stated boundary conditions, the derivation gives the static Green function 1/(4πr). Applying the existing gravitational source normalization yields the potential −μ/r, whose radial derivative gives the inward acceleration −μ/r². The note distinguishes potential, field amplitude, intensity, acceleration and optical measurement conversion, keeping geometric normalization separate from the distance exponent. The optical phase-ruler results are reviewed alongside the GRACE-FO forward forecasts. Calibrated reconstruction using measured phase retained micrometre-scale agreement with processed microwave ranging, while some forward models produced much larger errors. These results do not establish exponential error growth or identify a unique physical cause. The correspondence uses established mathematics and remains conditional on the supplied geometry, source calibration and physical interpretation. It does not establish an electromagnetic mechanism of gravity or derive spatial geometry from foundational Phase. The note includes the analytical proof, assumptions, evidence boundaries and requirements for a subsequent physical test. No new experimental data are introduced.
title: Inverse Radius Kernel and Optical Phase Registration

summary: This working paper develops a relational Phase interpretation of black holes within the Harmonic Physics research programme, using general relativity, exact Kerr geometry and semiclassical black-hole thermodynamics as its physical baseline. It examines how phase organisation, temporal reference, observer accessibility and information persistence might relate to black-hole closure. Within the proposed framework, a phase-cycle is a closed relational structure that supports recurrence. Measured succession requires distinguishable relations and persistent records, while geometry and causal history are treated as observer-level reconstructions. The temporal-anchor hypothesis concerns a deeper terminal condition at which the parent domain loses the internally usable references needed to resolve further clocks and geometry. This proposed condition is kept distinct from the regular event horizon, across which local evolution continues. Observation is described through a joint observation relation among admitted source organisation, a physical channel and an observer-capable organisation. Source state, coupling and registered record retain separate roles; changes in accessibility may alter registration while the source organisation persists. The paper consolidates three bounded mathematical findings: exact Kerr ingoing and outgoing endpoints can have opposite trapped and anti-trapped orientations with the same mass and spin parameters; spherical source/exterior matching leaves the transition law undetermined; and a leading slow-rotation calculation permits the same sign of angular momentum in closing and opening configurations. These results establish compatibility within the stated geometric constructions. A physical transition mechanism remains to be derived. Black-to-white-hole models provide external theoretical comparisons. Return to the original exterior and the opening of a daughter phase are treated as distinct hypotheses, each requiring an appropriate causal structure, state map and conservation accounting. The remaining requirements include an invariant parent-relative terminal criterion, a physical Phase-to-boundary map, transition dynamics, information and entropy accounting, and a stable nonperturbative rotating completion. The paper remains a developing theoretical interpretation supported by standard-geometry comparisons and bounded symbolic checks. It does not establish a physical black-to-white transition, information recovery through evaporation or a daughter universe. Version 2.3, dated 17 October 2026, updates observation and self-nesting terminology, clarifies geodesic incompleteness and fixed-angular-momentum assumptions, and refreshes the references. The existing displayed equations and reported test results are retained. keywords: Phase Theory; black holes; event horizons; geodesic incompleteness; relational time; phase contraction; information accessibility; singularity; white holes; quantum gravity.
title: Black Holes as Temporal Anchors

The core scale a = Lmax(Ncαs)^3/4 is generated dynamically by the termination of the Kolmogorov cascade. 3. The mass gap ∆YM =ℏcaκ1 is generated by the spontaneous mass permutation algebra of the Weyl group W(SU(Nc)) =∼ SNc operating on the tight horn torus geometry. 4. Color confinement follows from center-flux piercing statistics, establishing an area law with string tension σ > 0. This establishes a constructive, self-contained solution to the Clay Millennium problem in pure Yang–Mills theory.
title: Duality Between Classical Hamiltonian Yang–Mills Theory and the Non-Hamiltonian Vorton Basis: Spontaneous Mass Permutation at the Vorton Core

summary: This presentation offers a term for a harm that Ethnic Studies practitioners experience constantly and lack precise language for. It argues that the imprecision is itself a barrier to defense. Burnout is a convenient diagnostic category. It implies depletion from overwork, prescribes rest and strong boundaries, and locates the site of intervention in the self rather than the structure. This presentation argues that burnout functions as an institutional alibi. It recodes structural and relational injury as personal misalignment, and in doing so stabilizes the institution. Drawing on Foucault, the presentation shows how wellness discourse extends disciplinary power: workers become responsible for optimizing their own resilience within environments that remain unchanged. Burnout presumes excess. But what if the harm is not overextension but deprivation? Feminist ethics of care holds that care is a relational practice requiring response-ability. Without reciprocity, care becomes extraction. The presentation develops racialized relational starvation to name the chronic absence of reciprocal recognition, sponsorship, and institutional buffering in environments that nonetheless demand sustained care labor and loyalty. Asymmetry itself is not the injury. Fields are never flat. The distinction is between fluid asymmetry, where those holding institutional capital absorb risk and redistribute strain, and calcified asymmetry, where circulation stops and protection flows predictably in one direction. Stagnation is the greater harm, not simply hierarchy. Under these conditions, Ethnic Studies practitioners adapt through contortion: institutionally induced self-surveillance and anticipatory compliance, routinely misrecognized as professionalism and praised as diplomacy, composure, and reasonableness. The praise confirms the adaptation and leaves the conditions untouched. Sustained, contortion produces professional death, the cumulative erosion of ethical agency, epistemic confidence, relational participation, and pedagogical integrity, without formal departure. Those living it are the walking dead, structurally embedded, outwardly functioning, internally disengaged from the institution’s moral claims. Their continued presence lets the institution read survival as health. This is spirit murder in professional form, in the sense theorized by Love. It is not spectacle, but sediment, laid down through repetition. The presentation closes with a refusal of premature closure. It offers no reforms. To move quickly to prescription would rehabilitate the institution before the harm has been accounted for, converting accumulated injury into a problem of implementation. Where harm has been normalized and rendered ethically unintelligible, naming is not a step toward intervention. It is intervention. This is what a loving defense requires: the willingness to stay with what is happening long enough to name it precisely, and to refuse the comfort of solutions offered too soon. The presentation will be a twenty-minute talk with slides, moving through misnaming, starvation, contortion, and professional death, with the final minutes reserved for discussion. The vocabulary is offered as analytical scaffolding, and is only useful if others can test it against their own conditions and experiences.
title: Contortion Is Not Burnout: Racialized Relational Starvation and Professional Death in Ethnic Studies Work

summary: SELF-CALIBRATING NANO-NEURAL INTERFACES AND REFERENCE LINEAGE AT THE LIMIT Built-In References × Drift Attribution × Independent Functional Requalification STARLI / Institute XXIII / Research Flagship 17 PUBLICATION DESCRIPTION When a long-running neural interface changes, is the cause the sensor, the surrounding tissue, or the decoder? An adaptive algorithm can restore predictive accuracy while obscuring the physical origin of its own correction. This book proposes a rigorous, falsifiable architecture for self-calibrating nano-neural interfaces that must retain the scientific history of every reference and every update. Its central axiom is that self-calibration does not imply self-certification: measurement claims, permission to change, electrode safety and functional benefit demand independent evidence. The first coupling is the existence of physically traceable internal references that can be challenged against electrically and temporally independent standards. The second is a source-aware drift-diagnostic process that distinguishes electronics gain, electrode-tissue transfer, tissue-like surrogate changes, changing source signals and model/feature drift, explicitly recording instances of nonidentifiability. The third is external functional requalification, which can reject an apparently successful update after hidden-domain testing, material or reference replacement, loss of selectivity, missing raw observations, or inability to reproduce the frozen predecessor. This research monograph is divided into seven causal layers and 82 chapters. Five major subsections of each chapter are assigned independent pages, yielding 410 separately paginated technical essays. Thirty gold mathematical derivations are linked from chapter-opening equations to discriminating experiments. The mathematics includes augmented state-space observability, nonlinear observation functions, source-separation Jacobians, Kalman innovations, impedance spectroscopy, covariance propagation, change-point statistics, conformal coverage, selective risk, hard-veto constrained update eligibility, reference-bridge covariance, exact rollback and cross-laboratory requalification. A displayed formula is a candidate analytical instrument with stated dimensions and assumptions, not a discovered biological law. Two hundred detailed Research Gates are preserved at the rear: 82 interrogate source identifiability, another 82 challenge independent physical and evidential hard vetoes, and 36 require third-party reconstruction of a frozen reference history. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos propose revisable architectures, beginning with the Neural Interface Calibration Passport. The Passport ties an interface's physical identity to the raw analog and digitized record, calibrated unit chain, hardware reference ancestors, model and feature checksums, reasons for changing any reference, failed updates, revoked permissions, blinded requalification and rollback. These are proposed evidence structures, not commercially validated devices. The DOI bibliography contains 18 unique external research records covering chronic intracortical signal instability, low-dimensional BCI stabilization, decoder adaptation, long-term electrode-tissue behavior, complex impedance metrology, electrochemical reference limits, neural interface materials and conformal uncertainty under covariate shift. Selected publisher and PubMed pages were consulted for source metadata. Their findings cannot establish efficacy of the new self-calibration architecture; source-specific claims and independent replication would be necessary.

summary: This archive is the computational supplement for the manuscript “A five-qubit 1-resistant graph state and stabilizer marginal certificates” by Zicheng Han, Wanchen Zhang, and Xiande Zhang. It provides an exhaustive certificate-based classification of graph-state m-resistance for every connected local-Clifford (LC) class with N=5,...,11 vertices. One representative of each Danielsen LC class is included. For every representative, all admissible values m=0,...,N−2 are classified. For k=N−m−1, a graph state is accepted as m-resistant only when every k-vertex marginal has an explicit full-separability certificate and every (k+1)-vertex marginal has an explicit negative-partial-transpose (NPT) entanglement certificate. NPT certificates are obtained from exact integer Walsh spectra of partial transposes; no floating-point tolerance or analytical shortcut is used. The archive contains: - a self-contained Python classifier using only the Python standard library; - parsed representatives of all connected Danielsen LC classes for N=5,...,11; - one complete certificate record for every Danielsen class; - a decisive obstruction for every failed graph/m pair; - compact per-class and per-(N,m) summary tables; - provenance metadata and SHA-256 checksums. In total, 44,171 connected LC classes and 437,212 graph/m pairs were checked. The classification contains 20 RESISTANT decisions, 437,192 FAIL decisions, and zero UNKNOWN decisions. The resistant Danielsen classes are: - N=5: m=0, ID 5; m=1, ID 8. - N=6: m=0, ID 9; m=2, IDs 16, 18, and 19. - N=7: m=0, ID 20. - N=8: m=0, ID 46; m=3, IDs 138 and 142. - N=9: m=0, ID 147. - N=10: m=0, ID 587; m=4, IDs 3174, 3175, 3498, 3636, 3668, 3699, and 3701. - N=11: m=0, ID 3719. No other resistant classes were found. In particular, all 40,457 connected N=11 LC classes were checked for m=0,...,9. The only resistant N=11 representative is the m=0 class with Danielsen ID 3719, represented by the 11-vertex star; no N=11 class is resistant for m≥1. This version extends the earlier deposited materials by adding the complete N=11 classification and a consolidated, self-contained reproduction program. The Danielsen representatives originate from the Database of Entanglement in Graph States. Exact source URLs, citations, class counts, and source-file hashes are recorded in data/source_metadata.json.
title: Code and certificate data for "A five-qubit 1-resistant graph state and stabilizer marginal certificates"

summary: Overview This repository contains the two processed datasets analyzed in "Influence of land cover and shade on the thermal environments of schoolyards in Los Angeles" by Levinson et al. (in preparation). The data come from the LAUSD Cool Schoolyards experiment, a field study of how schoolyard surfaces affect surface temperature, air temperature, radiant heat, and outdoor thermal comfort at Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) elementary schools. The study compares four surface types: uncoated asphalt pavement, pavement with a high-reflectance coating (coated pavement), turf, and garden. The first file holds mobile measurements taken with an instrumented cart that was moved across each schoolyard. The second holds continuous measurements from three stationary weather stations placed over different surfaces. Study sites and measurement periods Each school is identified in the data by a two-letter code: HE : Harrison Elementary School, City Terrace, Los Angeles, CA BE : Braddock Drive Elementary School and Gifted Magnet, Culver City area, Los Angeles, CA SE : Saticoy Elementary School, North Hollywood, Los Angeles, CA Mobile cart measurements were made at HE on 2025-09-06, at BE on 2025-09-07, and at SE on 2025-09-14. The weather stations were deployed at BE from 2025-09-10 13:00 to 2025-10-10 09:00 and at HE from 2025-10-10 14:00 to 2025-11-02 00:00. File 1: Transect measurements Transect measurement stats at 1 min + coded transects + open-meteo weather + shade + LSH.csv An instrumented cart was moved along a route of numbered locations ("transect points") across each schoolyard. At each point it stopped for about one minute and recorded readings every second. Each row summarizes one stop, giving the mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum of every measured variable. The route was traversed repeatedly in forward and reverse directions. The file includes: Identifiers: school, measurement number, transect point, a tag of the form MMM_SS_PP (measurement number, school, point), transect number, and direction. Microclimate: air temperature, relative humidity, and wind speed and direction measured about 1.5 m above the ground. Radiation and surfaces: downward solar irradiance, ground albedo (the fraction of sunlight the ground reflects), ground surface temperature, sky temperature, and mean radiant temperature (MRT, a measure of the total radiant heat a person receives). Readings from 12 radiometers are also included: six measuring sunlight and six measuring longwave (thermal) radiation, facing up, down, forward, back, left, and right. Instrument orientation and position: radiometer tilt, roll, and zenith angles, plus GPS coordinates. Surface properties: surface description and classification of each point, along with measured solar reflectance and thermal emittance. Derived quantities: solar position, local solar hour, the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI, an index of how hot conditions feel to a person) and its heat-stress category, and a shade classification for each stop. In the Classification column, the labels "Warm pavement," "Cool pavement," "Grass," and "Nature area" correspond to uncoated pavement, coated pavement, turf, and garden, respectively. The file also gives air and ground temperature differences between stations: B−A (uncoated minus coated pav
