summary: This replication package accompanies the paper "An Exploratory Evaluation of Targeted Label Poisoning in a Client-Local Feature Federated Ensemble for Chest X-Ray Classification." It contains code and saved experimental results for an exploratory study of Pneumonia-to-Normal label poisoning in four-class chest X-ray classification. The study uses 20,795 images from three public sources, with 20,557 perceptual groups kept intact across experimental partitions. The package covers 212 completed training jobs, including main and component comparisons, classifier-head sensitivity, image-model references, candidate probability banks, and earlier-poisoning experiments. The main comparisons and image-model references use ten deterministic seeds. The classifier-head and GRU-structure study uses three seeds. Included materials comprise dataset manifests and image checksums, perceptual-group metadata, split assignments, seeds and configurations, held-out predictions, candidate probabilities, numerical summaries, result figures, analysis and verification scripts, and scientific execution-source snapshots. Additional fixed-model analyses examine validation availability, validation-label contamination, and artifact retention. The README and reproducibility guide explain verification, reanalysis, environment requirements, and dataset reconstruction. Dataset images and model checkpoints are not included. Obtain the source images separately under their applicable access and use terms: COVID-19 Radiography Database: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tawsifurrahman/covid19-radiography-database COVID19, Pneumonia, Normal Chest X-ray Images: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/sachinkumar413/covid-pneumonia-normal-chest-xray-images Tuberculosis Chest X-ray Dataset: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tawsifurrahman/tuberculosis-tb-chest-xray-dataset The included metadata identify the exact study images for reconstruction from the original source bytes. Saved results can be checked without source images or retraining. The attack direction was selected exploratorily, perceptual grouping does not establish patient independence, and source-held-out generalization was not evaluated. Reuse rights are described in LICENSE_STATUS.txt. This work was supported by the Deanship of Scientific Research (DSR) at King Abdulaziz University, Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, under grant No. IPP: 455-611-2026.
title: Replication Package for: An Exploratory Evaluation of Targeted Label Poisoning in a Client-Local Feature Federated Ensemble for Chest X-Ray Classification

summary: Version 3.0 is the final data and analysis package supporting the manuscript “Registration, Outcome Changes, and Results Dissemination in Dental Erosion Research: A ClinicalTrials.gov Meta-Research Study.” It preserves the ClinicalTrials.gov search, screening, extraction, registration, results-dissemination, and publication-matching materials based on the fixed October 14, 2026 data-freeze date (D0), and adds the completed historical-registry analysis. The historical-registry extension was added after completion of the initial D0 analysis. Its protocol addendum and coding rules were finalized on October 15, 2026 before study-specific historical-registry extraction and coding. The completed extension reviewed 200 ClinicalTrials.gov record-history versions across 42 interventional studies and identified 25 actual outcome-state transitions. Seven of 42 studies had at least one substantive primary-outcome change and two had a Major change. Historical registry–publication primary-outcome agreement was assessed for the 21 Definite publication matches. Final agreement was Complete in 15/21, Partial in 3/21, and No clear in 3/21 using both the historical baseline and the D0 registry record; no masked historical discrepancy was identified. Historical transition severity and historical registry–publication agreement were independently assessed by two reviewers before consensus. Differences were resolved through discussion and consensus, and final classifications were rechecked against the relevant ClinicalTrials.gov record histories and publication sources. Version 3.0 also includes the completed blinded independent Reviewer-2 worksheet, raw ClinicalTrials.gov record-history captures, final consensus/QC datasets, and SHA-256 checksums.
title: Data and Analysis Materials for ClinicalTrials.gov Meta-Research on Dental Erosion and Erosive Tooth Wear

summary: Large audio language models (LALMs) have made substantial progress in audio understanding. However, in high-throughput applications requiring frequent selection, judgment, and scoring, autoregressive text generation introduces additional computational overhead and response latency. To address this limitation, we introduce Qwen-Audio-Jev by augmenting Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next with a dedicated Jev decision head. The model unifies selection, binary judgment, and scoring through three decision primitives: CHOICE, NOUL, and SCORE. Given audio, a natural-language question, and an explicit answer specification, it directly produces a task-conditioned probability distribution or a numerical score through typed decision readouts. Evaluation across 18 labeled configurations covers all three primitives: for CHOICE, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves accuracies of 78.70% on MMAU-mini and 84.06% on MMSU; for NOUL, it achieves an equal error rate of 6.50% on the VoxCeleb1-O speaker verification benchmark; and for SCORE, the model achieves a normalized mean absolute error of 0.1062 on NISQA overall quality assessment, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of 0.8210 and 0.8074, respectively. Compared with the original Qwen-Audio-3.1-ASR-Flash-Next, Qwen-Audio-Jev achieves an approximately 20x inference speedup. It demonstrates its potential for efficient, high-throughput audio decision-making in applications such as large-scale audio screening, speaker verification, and automated quality assessment.
title: Qwen-Audio-Jev: A Unified Interface for Audio Decisions

summary: Neural instrument synthesizers can clone the timbre of a solo instrument, letting music producers make music with the sound they desire. However, an instrument of interest is often embedded in a fully produced, multi-instrument recording, beyond the reach of existing methods. Source separation before timbre cloning is an approach, but it may suffer from separation artifacts and is also likely a detour for the task. In this work, we propose Point-and-Play, a system that clones the timbre of a cued source directly from a polyphonic mixture and uses it to synthesize new pitches and velocities. To achieve this, we introduce a Cue-Gated Statistics Pooling (CGSP) module that extracts the timbre code of the cued instrument from adapted CLAP embeddings of the music mixture. This extracted timbre code is then used to condition a separately trained note synthesizer together with pitch and velocity inputs. Experiments show that our proposed system outperforms separate-then-clone baselines in terms of timbre fidelity and synthesis quality, achieving comparable performance with that cloned from a clean solo instrument.
title: Point-and-Play: Instrument Timbre Cloning from Music Mixtures

summary: Music source separation (MSS) has been conventionally addressed by discriminative methods. Recently, flow matching has emerged as a strong generative paradigm for modeling complex data distributions, with successful applications across diverse domains. These advances motivate us to systematically investigate flow matching for MSS in a four-source (Vocals, Bass, Drums, Other) setting in full-band stereo. Specifically, we investigate prediction targets, flow paths, single-source versus multi-source modeling, and mixture consistency constraints. Beyond the signal-level metrics commonly used for MSS, such as signal-to-distortion ratio, we further evaluate MSS methods using embedding-based metrics, as well as a listening test, providing a comprehensive benchmark. On MUSDB18-HQ, our proposed model exhibits competitive performance in both objective and subjective tests, highlighting the potential of flow matching for generative MSS. Demo: https://ik4sumii.github.io/FLOMSS/
title: FLOMSS: Generative Music Source Separation by Flow Matching

summary: Audio source separation models must preserve fine spectral structure while keeping the cost of the separator tractable. Band-split architectures reduce this cost by manually partitioning the spectrum into predefined frequency bands and encoding each band as a token, but the same boundaries are used for every mixture. Because informative spectral structure varies with source content, fixed boundaries can merge discriminative components or spend tokens where little resolution is needed. We introduce Dynamic Band Splitting (DBS), an end-to-end framework that adapts boundary locations and band widths to each mixture under a fixed band-token budget. DBS predicts content-conditioned boundary scores within frequency blocks, selects a prescribed number of boundaries using hard Top-$K$, and applies content-dependent pooling to obtain compact band tokens. After separation, it smooths and expands these tokens to the original STFT grid, refines them along frequency, and decodes complex masks with a frequency-shared head. DBS improved separation over the corresponding static models on DnR v2, MUSDB18-HQ, and EchoSet, with DBS-BSRNN achieving relative gain of 29.0% in average SI-SDR on DnR v2. These results and boundary analyses on DnR v2 show that content-adaptive frequency partitioning benefits multiple separator backbones under a fixed band-token budget. Code and audio demos are available at https://cslikai.cn/Dynamic-Band-Splitting
title: Learning Where to Split: Dynamic Band Splitting for Audio Source Separation

summary: Speaker verification (SV) systems now achieve very low error rates on standard public protocols, but those results do not fully describe deployment generalization. VoxCeleb-style evaluations remain useful anchors for English in-the-wild media speech. Scenario-specific evaluations and challenges are also valuable. However, neither setting directly shows whether the same system remains reliable across diverse deployment scenarios. We introduce OpenSVBench, a public benchmark for cross-scenario SV evaluation. Its fixed public core contains 26 trial sets organized into 11 scenario groups, with 9.15M verification trials, frozen target/non-target keys, and metadata for scenario-wise reporting. Around this core, the online leaderboard acts as a diagnostic evaluation interface rather than only a ranked list. It accepts score packages from new systems, evaluates them with frozen keys and common scoring, and reports trial-set breakdowns, scenario-group metrics, macro EER/minDCF, model-wise profiles, and scenario-wise comparisons. We evaluate 18 public checkpoints spanning x-vector, ECAPA-TDNN, CAMPPlus, ResNet and ERes variants, ReDimNet2, SAM-ResNet, and pretrained Transformer speaker recipes. The results show clear cross-scenario gaps: systems with similar macro EER can have different scenario profiles, strong performance in one scenario does not guarantee strong performance in another, and same-scenario trial sets can still expose source and protocol gaps.
title: OpenSVBench: Diagnosing Speaker Verification Generalization Across Deployment Scenarios

summary: Speech anonymization is evaluated with automatic speaker verification attackers whose performance depends on the attribute distribution of both their training and evaluation data, which may bias privacy estimates for some speaker groups. To alleviate this issue, we introduce VoxAnon, a dataset built from VoxCeleb1 and 2 with training and evaluation splits balanced across gender, age, accent, and pitch. We extract and cross-check attributes using two complementary methods, balance trial lists per subgroup, and draw test/enrollment utterances from distinct video sources in order to limit linguistic and session bias. Comparing VoxAnon with unbalanced training and test data across four attackers and three anonymizers, we show that attribute imbalance changes which subgroups appear hardest to re-identify, in directions that depend on the attribute. In the balanced setting, residual disparities persist, mostly tied to accent and pitch, and depend on the anonymizer/attacker pair. Code and trial lists are publicly available.
title: VoxAnon: A balanced dataset for a fair evaluation of speech anonymization

summary: This paper describes our systems for the Track 1 time-stamped speaker-attributed ASR task of the SmartGlasses Challenge. To handle overlapping speech, background noise and far-field conditions in two-person conversations, we employ SoulX-Transcriber, a multimodal large language model that takes full-length audio as input and generates structured transcriptions. In addition, we investigate the effect of speech frontend processing, including a rule-based Guided Source Separation method and a data-driven speech separation model, both of which improve performance on the validation set. Considering inference stability, our final submission uses the fine-tuned SoulX-Transcriber system, achieving a tcpCER of 6.22 on the test set.
title: Frontend-Assisted Large Audio-Language Models for SLT2026 SmartGlasses Challenge

summary: Spatial semantic segmentation of sound scenes (S5) jointly performs audio source separation and tagging on a multichannel audio mixture. Therefore, an S5 system can be decomposed into an audio tagging model and a separation model. The baseline S5 system in task~4 of the DCASE 2025 challenge uses M2D and ResUNet models for tagging and separation, respectively. These are large in overall size and therefore not appropriate for use in embedded devices. The main aim of this paper is to assess the performance loss in an S5 system when using lightweight tagging and separation models instead. To this end, we first compare the tagging performance of lightweight audio tagging models, namely PANNs and DyMNs, in terms of label prediction accuracy against the baseline M2D model. Secondly, we assess separation performance in terms of the scale-invariant signal-to-distortion ratio of the baseline ResUNet separator relative to that of a convolutional-based separator using SuDoRMRF. Finally, we combine the tagging and separation models across various configurations and assess the overall performance of the S5 system using the class-aware signal-to-distortion ratio.
title: Lightweight Systems for Spatial Semantic Segmentation of Sound Scenes

summary: Wearable augmented reality (AR) assistants are moving toward continuous real-world interaction, where they perceive the user's activity through first-person video and audio and provide timely spoken guidance without being explicitly asked. While proactive video assistants, spoken dialog systems, and egocentric task understanding have each advanced rapidly, existing systems do not address the joint problem of deciding when to speak and what to say from continuous first-person streams. We introduce EgoVoice, a framework for training and evaluating proactive egocentric spoken assistants. From HoloAssist video recordings of real human instructors, we construct clean audio streams through source separation and speech resynthesis, and convert each video session into a format where the model must decide at each moment whether to remain silent or provide spoken guidance. We fine-tune an omni-modal LLM with our data, and further improve its proactive intervention behavior with direct preference optimization. Experiments across closed and open-source models show that existing systems rarely produce well-timed, meaningful proactive interventions, while EgoVoice yields clear improvements in intervention timing, content relevance, and human preference over the zero-shot backbone.
title: EgoVoice: Proactive Spoken Assistance from Egocentric Multimodal Streams

summary: Speech remains intelligible to listeners under heavy temporal degradation, but whether speaker identity survives is largely unexplored. We evaluate six automatic speaker verification (ASV) models, trained on temporally intact speech, and tested under three degradations that remove different combinations of temporal cues. The models form three pairs, one per architecture family (convolutional, transformer, conformer), each pairing a waveform-input with a mel filterbank-input model. All models degrade, but robustness tracks input representation rather than pretraining scale or model size. In all nine family-by-condition comparisons the filterbank-input model degrades less, with eight of nine 95% confidence intervals excluding zero, even when it is smaller or has less pretraining than its waveform counterpart. In the controlled convolutional pair, where the models differ only in input representation, the filterbank-input model's equal error rate rises from 1.1% to 17.1% under the heaviest tested degradation, against 2.9% to29.7% for its waveform counterpart.
title: Input Representation, Not Model Size or Pretraining Scale, Shapes Speaker Verification Robustness to Temporal Degradation

summary: Blind Source Separation(BSS) is a fundamental problem in signal processing, aiming to separate multiple source signals from their mixtures without prior knowledge of the sources or the mixing process. Traditional approaches, such as Independent Vector Analysis (IVA) exploits statistical independence of sources. Recently, diffusion-based approaches have emerged as a promising alternative by leveraging powerful generative priors. Among them, ArrayDPS formulates BSS problem as a posterior sampling problem, and utilizes a pretrained speech diffusion model to guide the recovery of clean source signals. A key factor behind its separation capability is the multi-channel consistency (MC) objective, which enforces the estimated source signals to reconstruct the observed microphone mixtures through the estimated acoustic transfer functions. However, the number of microphones in the array is often limited, which constrains the performance of ArrayDPS. To address this issue, we propose VM-ArrayDPS, a novel method that augments the microphone array with virtual microphones with higher-SNR, these microphones can offer extra MC constraints to enhance the separation performance. Experimental results demonstrate that VM-ArrayDPS significantly outperforms ArrayDPS on both 2-speaker and 3-speaker datasets, showcasing the effectiveness of virtual microphone augmentation in improving BSS performance. We also did ablation studies to show the influence of the number of virtual microphones and weight of the MC objective brought by virtual microphones.
title: VM-ARRAYDPS: Virtual Microphone Augmented Diffusion Posterior Sampling for Unsupervised Blind Speech Separation

summary: Although room impulse responses (RIRs) encode source-distance cues, conventional monaural source separation focuses on recovering audio content without estimating source-specific RIRs, losing the associated spatial information. To address this limitation, we propose Distance-Aware Monaural Source Separation using Multi-RIR Estimation (DAMSEP), the first end-to-end framework that is jointly trained for source separation and multi-source RIR estimation from a single-microphone mixture. DAMSEP integrates a separation backbone with shared dereverberation and RIR estimation modules to jointly recover clean sources and source-specific complex convolutive transfer functions under source estimation and reverberant reconstruction objectives, enabling relative near/far ordering through the direct-to-reverberant ratios of the corresponding RIRs. For comprehensive evaluation, we introduce HETMIXR, which spans heterogeneous source content and diverse simulated room conditions with source-specific RIRs and geometric distance annotations. Experiments on HETMIXR demonstrate superior performance in source separation, RIR estimation, and distance ordering. Ablation studies reveal the complementary benefits of source supervision and reverberant reconstruction, while additional evaluations show generalization to single-speaker inputs and mixtures generated using measured RIRs from an unseen room. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Wenanzhi/DAMSEP.
title: DAMSEP: Distance-Aware Monaural Source Separation using Multi-RIR Estimation

summary: Discrete audio tokenization has become the critical interface between raw waveforms and autoregressive modeling in recent music generation. As a result, music tokenizers must simultaneously support high-fidelity reconstruction and produce discrete sequences that remain amenable to language modeling. Existing reconstruction-oriented tokenizers often mix musical structure with fine acoustic details, producing high-entropy tokens that are hard to model. In contrast, semantics-guided alternatives are designed for speech and do not fit music well, often hurting reconstruction quality. We address these trade-offs by rethinking music tokenization around a measurable notion of music semantic content grounded in downstream Music Information Retrieval tasks. Guided by this definition, we propose MuSeC, a music semantic codec that factorizes semantic and acoustic content directly from mixed signals without source separation. MuSeC preserves information required for high-fidelity reconstruction while producing more LM-friendly discrete units. Empirically, it improves reconstruction quality and yields more predictable token sequences, providing a practical foundation toward high-fidelity LLM music generation. Demos are available at https://longwaytog0.github.io/MuSeC/.
title: Rethinking Music Tokenization: A Semantic Codec toward High-Fidelity LLM Music Generation

summary: We present DECAF, a privacy preserving neural speech codec that obfuscates a speaker's voice while preserving linguistic content while maintaining automatic speech recognition (ASR) performance at very low bitrates, inspired by decaffeination. At the transmitter end, speech is encoded into speaker independent content embeddings, which are compressed using residual vector quantization and transmitted without any speaker related information. At the receiver, a canonical speaker embedding, shared a priori between endpoints, is used for waveform reconstruction, enabling deterministic and consistent obfuscation of a speaker's voice. The proposed framework leverages an information bottleneck applied to self supervised representations, along with a separate speaker embedding branch, to achieve effective speaker content disentanglement. We further incorporate a CTC-based auxiliary objective, encouraging content representations that are well aligned with downstream ASR tasks. We show that DECAF operating at a bit rate of 0.5 kbps achieves an Equal Error Rate (EER) of up to 43.5% for a speaker verification system, while maintaining competitive ASR performance, yielding a relative reduction in word error rate of 33.2% compared to a state of the art method.
title: Decaf: A privacy preserving speech codec using speaker disentanglement and canonical voice conversion

summary: Full-duplex speech models require training data that preserves turn-taking, overlap, interruption, and backchannel behavior, yet these signals are entangled across speakers in noisy real-world recordings. We present Conversational Voice, a pipeline that converts real two-speaker excerpts into three complementary training-data artifacts. (1) Separation recovers speaker-specific tracks with stable speaker assignments, a canonical transcript, and naturally observed interaction timing. (2) Reconstruction generates speech in matched voices from a fixed source transcript, reconstructs the source turn order, pauses, and overlaps, and adds word-level alignment and delivery instructions. (3) Expansion generates new dialogue constrained by the source context, speakers, and observed interaction pattern. Automatic speaker-verification metrics remain strong across stages, with same-speaker similarity of 0.983-0.991 and positive discrimination margins of 0.199-0.209. Predicted speech quality (NISQA MOS) is 3.56 for separation, 4.41 for reconstruction, and 4.61 for expansion. A Gemini-based automatic evaluator assigns expansion mean scores of 4.94/5 for contextual coherence and 4.80/5 for dialogue naturalness. Expansion and reconstruction exhibit broadly similar interaction profiles; expansion's turn, overlap-event, backchannel, and interruption rates are 4.6%, 8.0%, 13.2%, and 16.0% lower, respectively. We evaluate data properties only; downstream gains in full-duplex model training remain for future work.
title: ConversationalVoice: Full-Duplex Speech Data from Real Conversations through Source-Faithful Reconstruction and Conversation-Grounded Expansion

summary: Automatic Drum Transcription (ADT) is commonly formulated as a direct mapping from a music mixture to symbolic drum events. While effective for transcription, this formulation discards the acoustic stems that are useful for editing, remixing, and production. We revisit an alternative separate-and-detect formulation, where a drum source separation front end first produces five editable drum stems, and a fixed onset detector then converts each stem into symbolic events. The separator is built on a five-stem latent diffusion model that jointly generates kick, snare, toms, hi-hats, and cymbals in a compact VAE latent space. We further study two training-only auxiliary branches--an onset branch (OB) and a timbre branch (TB)--which shape the separator during learning but are discarded at inference. Trained on synthetic drum multitracks and evaluated on MDB Drums and ENST-Drums, the proposed pipeline consistently improves over a strong U-Net-based drum separation baseline in overall transcription F1. It also outperforms a representative end-to-end ADT system on kick and snare F1 under our evaluation protocol, while additionally providing separated audio stems. The ablation results show that OB gives the most stable transcription gains, whereas TB changes the trade-off between reconstruction, acoustic stem quality, and onset detection. These results suggest that generative drum demixing can serve not only as a source separation model, but also as a practical front end for interpretable drum transcription.
title: Separate-and-Detect: Unified Drum Transcription and Stem Generation via Latent Diffusion

summary: Acoustic-to-Articulatory Inversion (AAI) estimates vocal tract articulator movements from speech, benefiting tasks like ASR, speech synthesis, and speaker verification. While deep learning-based methods (CNNs, RNNs, Transformers) have advanced AAI, recent studies show that Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) features further enhance performance, particularly in low-resource settings. However, SSL feature extractors introduce inference latency and computational overhead. To address this, we propose a novel pretraining method leveraging three target representations-Phoneme Labels, Articulatory Feature Labels, and Critical-articulator Labels-eliminating the need for an SSL extractor during inference. We evaluate our approach against both baseline and SSL-based models across various data conditions. Results demonstrate that our method consistently improves AAI performance, particularly in low-resource scenarios, while significantly reducing inference costs without sacrificing accuracy.
title: Enhancing Acoustic-to-Articulatory Inversion with Multi-Target Pretraining for Low-Resource Settings

summary: Modern automatic speaker verification (ASV) systems are vulnerable to adversarial perturbations. Diffusion-based purification has recently shown strong effectiveness against such perturbations, but its reverse denoising process requires iterative sampling and leads to high inference latency. We find that the forward noising process provides most of the robustness gain. Motivated by this observation, we reformulate adversarial purification as a learnable noising problem, and propose the Positive-Incentive Noise Predictor (PnP), the first framework that explicitly introduces positive-incentive noise (π-noise) into the purification task. PnP learns input-adaptive π-noise and mixes it with the input to improve the robustness of downstream ASV systems. Experiments on four advanced ASV backbones show that PnP effectively defends against adversarial attacks while preserving performance on natural speech. Compared with representative purification baselines, the proposed framework provides a competitive balance among defense effectiveness, impact on genuine utterances, and inference efficiency under white-box, black-box, and defender-aware adaptive attacks, with a real-time factor as low as 0.014. Moreover, PnP can be cascaded with a diffusion denoiser to further improve the perceptual quality of purified utterances. Code and purified audio examples are available at https://eurecom-asp.github.io/pnp/
title: Positive-Incentive Noise Predictor for Adversarial Purification in Speaker Verification

summary: The goal of single-channel source separation is to reconstruct $K$ sources given their mixture. In supervised settings where vast amounts of clean source data are available, this challenging, ill-posed problem has been addressed successfully by generative diffusion and flow-based prior models. However, access to such clean source samples is often limited, and even when available, supervised models are vulnerable to domain shifts. To bridge this gap, we present Separation via Unsupervised Remixing Flow (SURF), an unsupervised flow matching approach for source separation that learns directly from observed mixtures. This method relies on a novel combination of state-of-the-art supervised flow matching and regression-based self-supervised techniques. At a high level, starting from a teacher model, we utilize a "remixing" step to bootstrap the learning of a student flow model from the teacher's estimates. We provide insights into the objectives optimized by this approach and draw a novel connection to the Wake-Sleep algorithm. Empirical evaluations on image and audio benchmarks demonstrate that SURF establishes a new state-of-the-art, significantly outperforming existing unsupervised methods. See our demo page for examples. https://google.github.io/df-conformer/surf/
title: SURF: Separation via Unsupervised Remixing Flow

summary: Distributed microphone arrays composed of multiple subarrays enable blind source separation over a wide spatial area. Directly applying fast multichannel nonnegative matrix factorization (FastMNMF) to all subarrays can exploit observations from all subarrays, but it requires repeated inversions of large matrices spanning all microphones, causing the computational cost to increase rapidly as the number of microphones grows. In contrast, applying FastMNMF to one subarray reduces the matrix size but cannot exploit observations from other subarrays. We propose distributed FastMNMF, which imposes a block-diagonal structure on the source spatial covariance matrices, so that matrix inversions are performed within subarrays. The NMF-based source spectrogram model is shared across subarrays, allowing the method to aggregate source activity information while discarding inter-subarray covariance. In synchronized, noiseless simulations with fixed room and array/source geometry, the method required less computation time than conventional FastMNMF using all subarrays, achieved a higher average source-to-distortion ratio than conventional FastMNMF using one subarray, and was applicable in the tested five-source condition, where each four-microphone subarray was locally underdetermined.
title: Fast Multichannel NMF with Block-Diagonal Spatial Covariance Matrices for Efficient Blind Source Separation Using Distributed Microphone Arrays

summary: Audio deepfakes generated by neural text-to-speech and voice-cloning systems threaten speaker verification and public discourse at scale. The core challenge is cross-dataset generalization: detectors trained on one synthesis pipeline collapse on unseen forgeries. We argue that this failure is primarily because of structural synthetic speech artifacts which are multi-timescale trajectory anomalies. Though every existing detector aggregates a fixed-window frame statistics, this misaligns the architecture with the signal. We propose FlowFake, a Liquid Time-Constant (LTC) architecture whose hidden state evolves via a learned ODE, with per-neuron adaptive time constants simultaneously resolving spectral (10ms) and prosodic (2s) cues. At only 34K parameters FlowFake achieves formal BIBO stability and O(dt^4) integration error. On a four-dataset cross domain benchmark (ASVspoof2019-LA, FakeOrReal, InTheWild, MLAAD), FlowFake reaches 75.29% on ASVspoof2019 trained only on FakeOrReal and 79.97% trained only on MLAAD. It outperforms RawGAT-ST and Whisper-DF on every evaluated pair and matching SSL Wav2vec2 (300x larger) at 0.01% of its parameter count. The source code is available on : https://github.com/GhostRider2023/FlowFake
title: FlowFake: Liquid Networks for Audio Deepfake Detection

summary: We propose DeepASA, a multi-purpose model for auditory scene analysis that performs multi-input multi-output (MIMO) source separation, dereverberation, sound event detection (SED), audio classification, and direction-of-arrival estimation (DoAE) within a unified framework. DeepASA is designed for complex auditory scenes where multiple, often similar, sound sources overlap in time and move dynamically in space. To achieve robust and consistent inference across tasks, we introduce an object-oriented processing (OOP) strategy. This approach encapsulates diverse auditory features into object-centric representations and refines them through a chain-of-inference (CoI) mechanism. The pipeline comprises a dynamic temporal kernel-based feature extractor, a transformer-based aggregator, and an object separator that yields per-object features. These features feed into multiple task-specific decoders. Our object-centric representations naturally resolve the parameter association ambiguity inherent in traditional track-wise processing. However, early-stage object separation can lead to failure in downstream ASA tasks. To address this, we implement temporal coherence matching (TCM) within the chain-of-inference, enabling multi-task fusion and iterative refinement of object features using estimated auditory parameters. We evaluate DeepASA on representative spatial audio benchmark datasets, including ASA2, MC-FUSS, and STARSS23. Experimental results show that our model achieves state-of-the-art performance across all evaluated tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness in both source separation and auditory parameter estimation under diverse spatial auditory scenes.
title: DeepASA: An Object-Oriented Multi-Purpose Network for Auditory Scene Analysis

summary: Singing Accompaniment Generation (SAG) is the process of generating instrumental music for a given clean vocal input. However, existing SAG techniques use source-separated vocals as input and overfit to separation artifacts. This creates a critical train-test mismatch, leading to failure on clean, real-world vocal inputs. We introduce AnyAccomp, a framework that resolves this by decoupling accompaniment generation from source-dependent artifacts. AnyAccomp first employs a quantized melodic bottleneck, using a chromagram and a VQ-VAE to extract a discrete and timbre-invariant representation of the core melody. A subsequent flow-matching model then generates the accompaniment conditioned on these robust codes. Experiments show AnyAccomp achieves competitive performance on separated-vocal benchmarks while significantly outperforming baselines on generalization test sets of clean studio vocals and, notably, solo instrumental tracks. This demonstrates a qualitative leap in generalization, enabling robust accompaniment for instruments - a task where existing models completely fail - and paving the way for more versatile music co-creation tools. Demo audio and code: https://anyaccomp.github.io
title: AnyAccomp: Generalizable Accompaniment Generation via Quantized Melodic Bottleneck

summary: The spoof speech detection (SSD) is the essential countermeasure for automatic speaker verification systems. Although SSD with magnitude features in the frequency domain has shown promising results, the phase information also can be important to capture the artefacts of certain types of spoofing attacks. Thus, both magnitude and phase features must be considered to ensure the generalization ability to diverse types of spoofing attacks. In this paper, we investigate the failure reason of feature-level fusion of the previous works through the entropy analysis from which we found that the randomness difference between magnitude and phase features is large, which can interrupt the feature-level fusion via backend neural network; thus, we propose a phase network to reduce that difference. Our SSD system: phase network equipped Res2Net achieved significant performance improvement, specifically in the spoofing attack for which the phase information is considered to be important. Also, we demonstrate our SSD system in both known- and unknown-kind SSD scenarios for practical applications.
title: Phase-Aware Spoof Speech Detection Based on Res2Net with Phase Network

summary: Automatic speaker verification (ASV) systems are highly vulnerable to presentation attacks, also called spoofing attacks. Replay is among the simplest attacks to mount - yet difficult to detect reliably. The generalization failure of spoofing countermeasures (CMs) has driven the community to study various alternative deep learning CMs. The majority of them are supervised approaches that learn a human-spoof discriminator. In this paper, we advocate a different, deep generative approach that leverages from powerful unsupervised manifold learning in classification. The potential benefits include the possibility to sample new data, and to obtain insights to the latent features of genuine and spoofed speech. To this end, we propose to use variational autoencoders (VAEs) as an alternative backend for replay attack detection, via three alternative models that differ in their class-conditioning. The first one, similar to the use of Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) in spoof detection, is to train independently two VAEs - one for each class. The second one is to train a single conditional model (C-VAE) by injecting a one-hot class label vector to the encoder and decoder networks. Our final proposal integrates an auxiliary classifier to guide the learning of the latent space. Our experimental results using constant-Q cepstral coefficient (CQCC) features on the ASVspoof 2017 and 2019 physical access subtask datasets indicate that the C-VAE offers substantial improvement in comparison to training two separate VAEs for each class. On the 2019 dataset, the C-VAE outperforms the VAE and the baseline GMM by an absolute 9 - 10% in both equal error rate (EER) and tandem detection cost function (t-DCF) metrics. Finally, we propose VAE residuals - the absolute difference of the original input and the reconstruction as features for spoofing detection.
title: Deep Generative Variational Autoencoding for Replay Spoof Detection in Automatic Speaker Verification

summary: In speech enhancement and source separation, signal-to-noise ratio is a ubiquitous objective measure of denoising/separation quality. A decade ago, the BSS_eval toolkit was developed to give researchers worldwide a way to evaluate the quality of their algorithms in a simple, fair, and hopefully insightful way: it attempted to account for channel variations, and to not only evaluate the total distortion in the estimated signal but also split it in terms of various factors such as remaining interference, newly added artifacts, and channel errors. In recent years, hundreds of papers have been relying on this toolkit to evaluate their proposed methods and compare them to previous works, often arguing that differences on the order of 0.1 dB proved the effectiveness of a method over others. We argue here that the signal-to-distortion ratio (SDR) implemented in the BSS_eval toolkit has generally been improperly used and abused, especially in the case of single-channel separation, resulting in misleading results. We propose to use a slightly modified definition, resulting in a simpler, more robust measure, called scale-invariant SDR (SI-SDR). We present various examples of critical failure of the original SDR that SI-SDR overcomes.
title: SDR - half-baked or well done?

summary: Speaker verification (SV) performance degrades under language mismatch due to the entanglement of speaker identity with language-specific acoustic cues. To address this problem, we leverage large-scale self-supervised pre-trained models (PTMs) to learn language-agnostic speaker representations. We utilize PTMs as robust front-end feature extractors, capitalizing on their rich acoustic and linguistic knowledge acquired from vast, diverse audio data. These generalized features are then used to train a downstream speaker embedding network, effectively disentangling speaker identity from language-specific characteristics. We validate our approach on the TidyVoice2026 benchmark, which benchmarks SV under language mismatch. Our proposed system (team T02) achieves equal error rates (EERs) of 2.21% on tv26_eval-A and 2.99% on tv26_eval-U.
title: Cross-Lingual Speaker Verification with Self-Supervised Pre-Trained Models

summary: Language-queried audio source separation (LASS) enables extracting any sound source using natural language. However, adapting LASS models to application-specific sound classes is challenging due to noisy training data and limited semantic coverage of the CLAP-based control signals. We propose a framework comprised of an automated data engine for training-data curation and a two-stage optimization process for class-specific CLAP control signals. Our objective evaluations across seven sound classes show that data refinement and control signal optimization consistently improve source separation performance. Subjective evaluation with 17 participants further demonstrates perceptual improvements of the model trained with optimized control signals over baseline and similar commercial models.
title: A Study on Improving Multi-class Audio Source Separation Via Decoupled CLAP Query Optimization and an Automated Data Engine

summary: Embedding enhancement improves speaker verification under acoustic mismatch without modifying a frozen backbone. Recent work has established a practical label-free setting for this task, but often adopts increasingly structured formulations. Here, the clean target is directly observed during training, making enhancement a matching problem on the unit hypersphere. We model the clean target with a von Mises--Fisher (vMF) likelihood and profile out a sample-wise concentration parameter, yielding a simple closed-form objective with adaptive weighting. Across VoxCeleb1, VoxSRC23, CN-Celeb, VOiCES, and VC-Mix, the proposed method largely preserves the baseline and gives clearer gains on challenging mismatch sets. It also remains stable under a broad single-view recipe, where a recent diffusion baseline becomes less reliable in controlled comparisons. These results suggest that effective label-free embedding enhancement in this setting does not require a highly structured formulation.
title: Revisiting Label-Free Speaker Embedding Enhancement with vMF Profile Likelihood

summary: Speech-pretrained models have shown promise in animal bioacoustics, but the factors governing their cross-species transfer remain poorly understood. We evaluate 15 frozen encoders spanning monolingual and multilingual speech, speaker verification, animal bioacoustics, and general audio on caller identification across four species and call-type classification across three. Differences between the strongest speech- and animal-pretrained representations range from $-0.027$ to $+0.119$ UAR; speech is significantly better in three of seven settings ($p<0.01$) and not significantly different in the remaining four. Controlled comparisons show no systematic advantage from increased language coverage or animal-domain pretraining, while frozen speaker-verification embeddings transfer poorly. The results also show that transfer is strongly layer-dependent: raw-waveform models peak early, whereas patch-spectrogram models peak deeper.
title: Neural Representations, Natural Connections: What Transfers From Human Speech Foundation Models to Animal Vocalizations?

files.key: Most of what you call your life arrives half a second late^L (1).docx

summary: C. J Tully. Independent Research https://orcid.org/0009-0007-5661-7332 chloetully5@gmail.com   18 th October 2026                   Most of what you call your life arrives half a second late. Something happens. A sound, a face, a tightness in the chest. Before you have chosen anything, a voice — yours, apparently — has already named it, judged it, and filed it under a chapter called me. You do not notice the filing. You notice the file. And so you spend your days inside a commentary about a world you have not, strictly speaking, met. This is not a moral failure. It is a timing error. Awareness is not a mood you work up and not a belief you adopt. It is what is already underway before the sentence starts. The breath you are taking does not consult your biography. The light on the wall does not ask what you meant to become. For a fraction of a second there is contact without a commentator. Then the commentator returns, a little late, a little proud, and explains what just occurred as if the explanation were the event. People talk about waking up as if it were a prize for the patient and the pure. It is closer to catching a clerical mistake. You have been treating the report as the room. The report is useful. It gets you across streets, through grief, into love, out of traffic. It is also not the thing it reports on. The word water has never once made a hand wet. Watch the exact moment a thought claims you. There is a sensation, then a grab. The grab feels like identity. It is older than that, and thinner. It is a habit of ownership so practiced it forgot it was optional. You do not have to defeat it. You only have to notice that noticing is already happening, and that the one who seems to be doing the noticing cannot be found as an object inside what is noticed. Sit with that past the point of comfort. Comfort is how the narration gets rehired. If the “you” who plans, defends, remembers, and suffers is a pattern appearing in awareness, then who has been afraid all this time? Not a cosmic answer. A local one. Look. Fear is weather. The sky it crosses was not manufactured by the storm. Nothing theatrical follows from this. You will still want things. You will still lose them. You will still answer the message and miss the person. The only change is a small, stubborn order of operations: experience first, story second. And the recognition, quiet enough to miss if you perform it, that you were never inside the story. You were the place it was being told. That place does not improve. It does not arrive. It does not need you to become someone else in order to be what it already is. The only work, if it can even be called work, is to stop leaving a half-second early — to remain, once, with what is here before you agree with your own explanation of it. Stay. The explanation can wait. It always could.
title: Most of what you call your life arrives half a second late.

summary: Code and data to reproduce all analyses and the figure in Sellers et al. (2026) “Failure of a tropical upwelling rapidly collapsed Panama’s anchoveta fishery and its exports”. Includes Python scripts for the bay-wide composite upwelling index, the observer set records, the unified 1956 to 2025 landings series, the main figure, and every statistic reported in the paper and its Supporting Information. Data include weekly sonde casts from the three deep central stations of the Bay of Panama, reef temperature loggers in the Gulf of Panama running since 1995, the Copernicus Marine Service biogeochemical reanalysis of net primary production (1994 to 2026), anchoveta and thread herring landings spliced from the digitised national stock assessment (1956 to 2014) and the ARAP landings register (2015 to 2025), 3,077 onboard observer purse-seine set records (2017 to 2025), 645 dockside proximate assays of landed anchoveta (2016 to 2025), and fish oil and fishmeal export tabulations from INEC customs statistics (1997 to 2025). Version 2.0 accompanies the revised manuscript and corrects three errors in version 1.0 (the units of the 1956 to 2005 landings, a wrongly masked grid cell in the production analysis, and a duplicated logger record), as listed in README.md. Data are released under CC BY 4.0 and code under the MIT Licence.
title: Code and data for: Failure of a tropical upwelling rapidly collapsed Panama's anchoveta fishery and its exports

summary: The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority examines a problem of institutional AI: automated decisions can scale faster than institutions' capacity to justify, reconsider, correct, or repair them. Identifying a responsible institution does not establish that its decisions were warrantedly adopted or that resulting obligations can be discharged. Across philosophy of language, social epistemology, social ontology, normative theory, AI governance, and administrative law , the monograph develops a substrate-neutral Discursive Ontology connecting three questions: who bears an institutional commitment, what warrants its adoption, and whether answerability can be sustained at scale. It distinguishes commitment ownership, warranted adoption, adequate discharge, causal contribution, and legal liability. Five contributions follow: Discursive Ontology and Answerability. Defines commitment-bearing through four jointly necessary relations within reciprocal normative standing: attribution continuity, challenge-responsive reconsideration, repair competence, and standing-consequence . It distinguishes Actual, Residual, Prospective, and Empty Occupancy . Empty Occupancy requires presentation as an independent bearer and affirmative evidence that the relevant standing is absent , not a mere machine interface. The axiom is that missing bearership is not defective ownership : a principal may remain responsible for commitments its interface cannot independently bear. Testimony Without a Testifier. Separates hearer-side epistemic uptake from speaker-side commitment ownership . Machine outputs can inform without establishing an answerable speaker. On assurance-based accounts, they can exercise testimonial force without constituting testimony . Reliability, fluency, and conversational memory alone confer no authority to retract a commitment. Normative Sponsorship. Specifies five conditions for warranted institutional adoption: epistemic access, authority, review bandwidth, independent rejection, and repair power . Its contestation-grain opacity threshold requires reconstructing relevant grounds where a challenge must take effect—at input, case, rule, shared-premise, or architecture—without complete transparency. It distinguishes technical opacity from organizational capture , where reasons are knowable but cannot bind, and considers model succession and agentic chains. Deontic Debt and Institutional Insolvency. Derives consequence-sensitive reconsideration from the defeasibility of presumptive authority. Deontic Debt comprises matured obligations deficiently serviced, not simply pending work. Institutional Insolvency arises when no credible service plan meets relevant obligations and protections for a specified claim mix, issuance scale, lawful architecture, and horizon. Its consequence is targeted loss of presumptive authority , not automatic legal invalidity or release from ownership and repair duties. Institutional Stewardship. Connects permissible automated use to warranted sponsorship, protective review, binding reconsideration, and effective repair. Restoration requires legacy discharge, demonstrable future capacity, and scaled resumption. Public-record analyses examine Australia's Robodebt scheme, Moffatt v. Air Canada , A.M.C. v. Smith (TennCare), the Post Office Horizon scandal, the Dutch childcare-benefits affair, and a press-based DPD generative-interface episode. Neither Air Canada nor DPD establishes determinate Empty Occupancy. An explicitly fictional, stipulated Meridian–Aster appeals-agent comparator yields a determinate verdict: Aster lacks independent standing while its insurer, Meridian, remains the Actual institutional bearer. This is not empirical evidence and settles neither sponsorship nor serviceability. A stipulated positive comparator illustrates review and repair. Objections address synthetic agency, status conferral, intentionality, human–machine parit
title: The Empty Occupant: Answerability, Testimony, and the Limits of Machine-Mediated Authority

summary: We develop a rigorous finite-dimensional mathematical framework connecting the renormalization group, gradient flows, Lyapunov stability, and noncooperative game theory. The central object is a renormalization-group flow written in gradient form, dg_i/dt = β_i(g) = - ∑_j G_ij(g) ∂Γ/∂g_j(g),          (1) where g = (g_1, …, g_n) belongs to an open domain M ⊂ ℝⁿ, Γ is a C² function, and G(g) is a symmetric positive-definite matrix. We associate to this flow a common-payoff game whose payoff is U(g) = - Γ(g).                   (2) We prove, with complete arguments, that ordinary Nash equilibria always imply renormalization-group fixed points, but the converse is false. We then identify the exact condition under which a fixed point becomes a genuine stable equilibrium of the game: a nondegenerate renormalization-group fixed point is asymptotically stable if and only if the Hessian of Γ is positive definite, if and only if it is a strict local minimum of Γ, if and only if it is a strict strong Nash equilibrium of U = -Γ. The distinction between ordinary Nash equilibrium and strong Nash equilibrium is essential. Ordinary Nash equilibria allow only unilateral deviations, while strong Nash equilibria exclude all small joint deviations. We provide explicit counterexamples showing that fixed points need not be Nash equilibria, that ordinary Nash equilibria need not be stable, and that invertibility of G alone does not imply finiteness of equilibria. We also prove global existence results under compactness and finiteness results under Morse nondegeneracy. The paper is self-contained at the level of multivariable calculus, linear algebra, ordinary differential equations, and basic Lyapunov stability theory. The framework is intentionally conditional: it does not claim that the gradient-flow representation has been proven in four-dimensional QCD or in any specific quantum field theory. Those issues are placed in a final section of open problems.
title: Gradient-Flow Renormalization Group as a Common-Potential Game: A Rigorous Equivalence Between Asymptotically Stable Fixed Points and Strict Strong Nash Equilibria

summary: We develop a rigorous reduction inside the Connes–Consani–Moscovici programme for the Riemann hypothesis. The main unconditional result is the following symmetry principle: for the truncated Weil quadratic form QW_λ^N, simplicity of the lowest eigenvalue ε_N implies evenness of the corresponding ground state ξ, provided the natural reflection symmetry γV_n = V_{-n} and the normalization ℓ_N(ξ) = 1 are imposed. This converts two structural requirements of the programme into one spectral requirement. We then prove a precise spectral approximation criterion. If the finite-dimensional form QW_λ^N approximates the prolate wave operator PW_λ in a form-strong sense sufficient to preserve the first isolated simple eigenvalue, then ε_N is simple for all large N. Combining this criterion with the symmetry principle gives evenness of the ground state. Finally, we prove a windowed determinant criterion for the Riemann hypothesis. If the regularized determinants attached to the Connes–Consani–Moscovici finite-rank perturbations have only real zeros and converge locally uniformly, on an exhausting family of windows, to nonzero multiples of the Riemann Ξ-function, then every zero of Ξ is real, and therefore the Riemann hypothesis follows. The paper separates cleanly the proved logical reductions from the analytic objectives required for their unconditional verification. Those objectives are collected in a final section of open problems, giving a foundational reference for the remaining work in the programme. We emphasize that this paper does not claim an unconditional proof of the Riemann hypothesis; rather, it provides a precise structural reduction and isolates the remaining analytic challenges.
title: Evenness from Simplicity in the Truncated Weil Quadratic Form and Conditional Spectral Criteria for the Riemann Hypothesis

summary: International business (IB) theory explains how firms enter foreign markets, allocate ownership, govern cross-border activities, build networks, and accumulate market knowledge. Less explicit attention has been given to the internationalization of the firm’s continuing operating system itself. This article develops the concept of operational internationalization: the cross-border extension of recurring fulfilment, inventory, logistics, service, compliance, and information processes, regardless of whether the underlying capabilities are fully owned by the focal firm. It further introduces operational embeddedness and boundary asymmetry to explain why ownership, governance, operational, and jurisdictional boundaries may overlap without expanding synchronously. Sovereign jurisdiction is treated as a constitutive boundary because tax, customs, data, product, environmental, and related rules shape which cross-border configurations are institutionally admissible. The framework becomes dynamic through reverse value-information flow, whereby economically consequential market and jurisdictional information generated abroad enters subsequent production, allocation, service, and organizational decisions. Just-in-Place (JIP) is positioned within this architecture as the enactment logic through which geographically and institutionally dispersed capabilities are selectively activated and recombined. A comparative public-disclosure analysis of Linamar and JD Logistics provides complementary evidence of inward informational feedback and outward operational extension. The article reconceptualizes internationalization as a reflexive, multi-boundary process in which the operating system itself becomes an analytically distinct object of cross-border expansion.
title: Internationalizing the Operating System: Operational Embeddedness, Jurisdictional Boundaries, and Just-in-Place

summary: No contexto atual de valorização das práticas sustentáveis e da eficiência operacional, a logística reversa apresenta-se como uma ferramenta estratégica na gestão de resíduos sólidos em ambientes aeroportuários. O presente estudo tem como objetivo analisar os principais desafios relacionados à logística reversa no Aeroporto Internacional de São Paulo/Guarulhos, bem como avaliar o uso de tecnologias aplicadas à logística como forma de otimização dos processos. A metodologia adotada baseia-se em revisão bibliográfica e análise de estudos de caso. Os resultados demonstram que a ausência de um sistema integrado de gestão de resíduos, aliada à baixa utilização de tecnologias, compromete a eficiência operacional e gera perdas financeiras. Como proposta, sugere-se a implantação de um sistema inteligente de monitoramento de resíduos com uso de Internet das Coisas (IoT), visando aumentar a eficiência da coleta seletiva e o reaproveitamento de materiais.
title: Logística Reversa e Tecnologia Aplicada no Aeroporto Internacional de Guarulhos: Desafios e Soluções Operacionais

summary: We study diagonal infinite-order operators on the flat torus of the form P = A(|D|),                        (1) where D = -i∇ is the momentum operator on T^n and A: [0,∞) → (0,∞) is a positive radial symbol with super-polynomial growth. Under explicit log-convexity and steepness assumptions on A, we prove a Weyl law for the eigenvalue counting function, a leading heat-kernel asymptotic, and the small positive-s behavior of the spectral zeta function. The main proved results are the following. 1. Weyl law with an elementary remainder: N_P(λ) = C_n (A^(-1)(λ))^n + O((A^(-1)(λ))^(n-1)), λ → ∞,                                 (2) where C_n = ω_n/(2π)^n, ω_n = π^(n/2)/Γ(n/2 + 1).           (3) 2. Leading heat-kernel asymptotic: Tr(e^(-tP)) = C_n (R(t))^n (1 + o(1)), t → 0+,           (4) where R(t) is defined by A(R(t)) = 1/t.                    (5) 3. Zeta asymptotics in terms of the inverse growth function. Define G(u) = (A^(-1)(e^u))^n.  (6) Assume that, as u → ∞, G(u) ~ u^ρ L(u), where ρ ≥ 0 and L is slowly varying. If ρ = 0, assume also that G(u) → ∞. Then, as s → 0+, ζ_P(s) ~ C_n Γ(ρ + 1) s^(-ρ) L(1/s). 4. For the model symbols A(r) = exp(l r^q), l > 0, q ≥ 1,                                       (7) and, more generally, A(r) = exp^(k)(l r^q), k ≥ 2, l > 0, q > 0, we obtain explicit asymptotics. If d = n/q, then:                                  (8) For depth k = 1:               (9) N_P(λ) ~ C_n l^(-d) (log λ)^d, Tr(e^(-tP)) ~ C_n l^(-d) (log(1/t))^d, ζ_P(s) ~ C_n l^(-d) Γ(d + 1) s^(-d). For depth k ≥ 2: N_P(λ) ~ C_n l^(-d) (log^(k) λ)^d, Tr(e^(-tP)) ~ C_n l^(-d) (log^(k)(1/t))^d, ζ_P(s) ~ C_n l^(-d) (log^(k-1)(1/s))^d. Here exp^(1)(x) = e^x, exp^(k+1)(x) = exp(exp^(k)(x)), log^(1)(x) = log x, and log^(k+1)(x) = log(log^(k)(x)). The paper proves only statements that are fully justified in the diagonal commutative model. Noncommutative residue theory, decomposition assumptions, spectral triples, local residue pairing formulas, integrality statements, and topological residue theorems are not proved here and are listed as open problems.
title: HEAT KERNEL, WEYL LAW, AND ZETA ASYMPTOTICS FOR DIAGONAL INFINITE-ORDER OPERATORS WITH SUPER-POLYNOMIAL GROWTH

summary: Code, trained weights and campaign results for the paper "Morphological diffusion by ball births: generative models of binary images with exact Betti increments" by M. Zéraï, submitted to the Journal of Mathematical Imaging and Vision. The model generates binary images by births of maximal balls. Its forward process is a random granulometry, and its reverse process learns a birth map. morpho_repro.tar.gz contains the implementation (model, sampler, exact Euler increments, measurement protocol), the averaged (EMA) weights of all trained models on the three datasets (GRF, BBBC039 nuclei masks, MNIST), the campaign reports and logs, and the GRF data. README.md gives the hyperparameters, the source of each table and the reproduction commands. figs_print.tar.gz contains the figure boards of the paper with their statistics. The BBBC039 masks and MNIST are public and are downloaded by prepare_data.sh. Note: the two archives are gzip-compressed tar files, deposited as morpho_repro.tar and figs_print.tar (README.md names them morpho_repro.tar.gz and figs_print.tar.gz). Extract them with: tar xzf morpho_repro.tar
title: Morphological diffusion by ball births: code, trained weights and campaign results

summary: Region means and contrasts with a full error budget, correlated shift errors, error bars for shot noise, a faster fit_map , two tutorials, and three fixes. Added region_mean(coefficients, dw1, dw2, sigma1, sigma2, mask, *, shift_correlation=None, ref_sigma=None) and region_contrast(coefficients, dw1, dw2, sigma1, sigma2, mask_a, mask_b, *, shift_correlation=None) , returning a RegionEstimate : the mean strain and density of a map region, or region A minus region B, with the error split into shift noise (averages down over pixels), calibration (from a two-mode CalibrationResult ; does not average down) and reference frequencies ( ref_sigma ; does not average down, and cancels exactly in a contrast). region_mean also tests whether the pixels agree within their error bars (chi-square with 2 (N - 1) degrees of freedom, the same in shift space and in (strain, density) space) and reports the pixel spread. Validated against the mean and per-pixel covariances of SeparationModel.invert , separation_with_calibration , finite differences of a re-solve, and seeded Monte Carlo over 400 trials that repeat the calibration, the map noise and the reference error (spread within 12 % of the reported error bars). Propagation as in JCGM 100:2008 (GUM), 5.2.2, Eq. (13). SeparationModel.invert(..., shift_correlation=None) : the correlation of the two shift errors (from a joint fit) enters the error bars through the full 2 x 2 shift covariance. Zero gives the old result bit for bit. On 400 repeats of two overlapping E' + A'1 peaks the density error bar without the correlation is 27 % above the actual spread; with it, it matches (tutorial 2). separation_with_calibration passes it through. MapFitResult.shift_correlation : the correlation of the two shift errors per pixel (the joint fit's value, 0 for separate window fits, NaN where masked). noise="varying" in fit_lorentzian , fit_two_modes and fit_map : error bars from the heteroskedasticity-consistent ("sandwich") covariance of H. White, Econometrica 48, 817 (1980), for spectra whose noise level changes along the axis, as shot noise does. Fitted values are unchanged. On 600 seeded Poisson spectra the center scatter is 1.7 times the default error bar and within 10 % of the new one; checked also against an independent finite-difference sandwich (relative 1e-5). The default, noise="constant" , is unchanged. README example 18 (shot noise) and a "Tutorials" section. Fixed calibrate_lever_arms , plan_calibration and design_references judged identifiability from the raw singular values of the design, which depends on the units. Before: the six-state design of the tests with the density in cm^-2 raised ValueError: reference states are collinear ... ( plan_calibration returned identifiable=False ). After: it gives the arms of the fit in 1e13 cm^-2, rescaled (A'1 density arm -2.2798e-13 per cm^-2 against -2.2798 per 1e13 cm^-2; relative 1e-10). The test is now made on the design with unit-length columns (also with fit_offset=True ). Test: test_calibration_does_not_depend_on_the_density_unit , test_planning_does_not_depend_on_the_density_unit . bayesian_map_inversion(..., fill_masked=True) : the same unit dependence in its pooled-information check. summary: Hashing, signing, and timestamping establish that a document has not changed. When a legal document is produced by composition, from templates, clause libraries, shared definitions, and parameters that evolve independently, the governing text is a resolved state, and the integrity of the root document does not ensure that this state can be reconstructed. We treat this as a problem of ex post auditability. We define the resolved state as S_t = ρ(A_0, R_t, C_t), derive five properties of its auditability from requirements established in archival science, legal document standards, and norm-change formalisms, and introduce a capture model K_t with a diagnostic procedure that reports which properties a capture fails. We implement the framework in cmacc-attest and apply it to the 175 instantiated contracts of the CommonAccord library. References resolve in 96.6% of contracts, yet none is auditable: no reference is version-locked, and 98.3% contain conflicts settled by an unattested precedence order. Replaying 194 commits of the library history shows that 88.5% of the changes in resolved contracts left the root file unchanged. Repository history narrows reconstruction when the time of resolution is known, but does not replace a capture.
title: Beyond Document Integrity: Auditing Resolved States of Formalized Legal Documents

summary: MULTI-AGENT ROUTING OF NEUROVASCULAR MICROROBOT SWARMS AT THE LIMIT This research monograph develops a falsifiable, non-clinical framework for routing heterogeneous microrobotic teams through branching neurovascular vessel phantoms. It asks whether decentralized task assignment, flow-aware navigation, independently tracked agent identity, and verifiable recovery can improve qualified sensing or inert-sample collection without increasing collision, occlusion, flow disturbance, thermal burden, sample confusion, or residual material risk. Organized around low-Reynolds-number hydrodynamics, multi-agent coordination, and independently enforced physical safety boundaries, the volume contains 30 mathematical derivation plates, 82 full research chapters with five separately paginated sections each, 200 detailed Research Gates, and 33 provisional Phoenix Answer Embryos. A DOI evidence ledger distinguishes established component physics and published demonstrations from the original system-level hypotheses proposed here. Strong passive-transport, single-agent, and information-matched centralized alternatives remain valid competitors throughout. Research failures, abandoned models, experimental uncertainty, and successor reconstruction are treated as scientific outputs, not editorial defects. The monograph provides a research architecture and prospective tests, not results from experiments performed for this publication. It does not assert demonstrated autonomous navigation in human cerebral vessels, clinical safety, therapeutic efficacy, or authorization for human intervention.

summary: Absorption and scattering coefficients for the Jerlov optical water types, taken from the primary literature with the provenance of every value recorded. Values that a published table got wrong are flagged rather than silently repaired, and quantities the data do not determine are refused rather than guessed. Twenty-three entries are documented, nine of them confirmed defects in the source literature: duplicated rows in Solonenko & Mobley (2015) Table 7, a transcription error in the small-particle scattering coefficient that propagated into their published coefficients, a Data Availability Statement that gives the DOI of an unrelated dataset, and a reprint whose stated unit is out by a factor of ten. Three further entries were open questions that obtaining the 1968 first edition settled. The same Jerlov water type is in circulation with beam attenuations differing by a factor of five, which is why every coefficient here carries the source it came from. Every shipped table can be regenerated from its primary source by the scripts in tools/ , and each generation step checks the result against the equations of the paper it came from. The package computes the direct and veiling components along a horizontal underwater path, converts spectra to CIE XYZ, sRGB, or the response of an arbitrary camera or set of photoreceptors, gives the Jerlov type that typically applies in each 10 m layer down to 200 m and carries the downwelling irradiance down through those layers, integrates photosynthetically available radiation (PAR), or the photon flux over any other band or weighted by any spectral sensitivity, with depth, gives the spectrum at any depth and the effective Kd between two, and finds the depth at which PAR falls to 1 percent, ranks the Jerlov types by their distance from a measured Kd spectrum, carries Jerlov's measured profiles of quanta irradiance (350-700 nm) by water type and checks the depth profile against them, carries Tyler's (1958) measured radiance distribution in Lake Pend Oreille, carries the Paulson & Simpson (1977) shortwave penetration parameters used by ocean circulation models, converts a backscattering sensor's single-angle reading into the backscattering coefficient, and carries Petzold's (1972) volume scattering functions for eight measured ocean waters.
title: jerlov: inherent optical properties of the Jerlov optical water types, with provenance

summary: Unrefereed AI-assisted mathematical candidate for the iid prophet inequality over time with arbitrary lease durations. The unrestricted asymptotic ratio exists and lies in [0.60922, 0.609816], below the inverse golden ratio. Written analytic arguments and Arb numerical certificates have distinct assurance scopes. Producer replay and negative controls do not establish external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification. Original prose and data are CC0-1.0; original code is MIT licensed.
title: The optimal i.i.d. prophet inequality over time is not the inverse golden ratio

summary: Coding agents can now interpret a specification, implement it, write and execute tests, repair failures, and declare the result ready for release. When the same agentic system produces both the software and the evidence of its correctness, a passing test suite no longer constitutes independent evidence. Visible tests become an optimization target, and code, tests, and oracles may share a single misinterpretation of the specification. This paper argues that agent-produced software requires an assurance plane that is structurally independent of the build plane. We first characterize four gaps along the chain from stakeholder intent to production, namely the requirement, conformance, evaluation, and model gaps, and identify which of them verification can close. We then propose a framework that separates building from verifying, introduces a Verification Contract stating what must be demonstrated before release, and organizes verification in two phases: a specification-first phase designed without access to the implementation, and an implementation-aware phase that strengthens the evidence through mutation analysis, property-based testing, and fuzzing. The resulting evidence is consolidated into an assurance report that makes residual uncertainty explicit and leaves the release decision to a human. We evaluate the framework in a pre-registered study on three stateful services, two of them written by third-party models, and an EvalPlus pilot, comparing self-validation with independent verification under context-level and model-level independence. The builder's programs were correct, but its own tests missed subtle interactions: a verifier in a fresh context detected more of the 46 seeded faults than the builder's tests (Holm-corrected p = 0.006), and surfaced the ambiguities of the specification, at the price of rare false oracles. A verifier from another provider did not add detection. The framework and the study provide a basis for governing the release of software produced by agents.
title: Who Verifies the Builder? Toward Independent Assurance for Agent-Produced Software

Zhang, Gauge Field Fluctuations Protect the Higgs Vacuum When a Small Universe Begins (2026), a Letter; A. Zhang, A Casimir turning point as the beginning of a small flat universe (2026). Zhang, Casimir Cosmology: Derivations and Numerical Validation, version 1.0 (2026), is deposited as a separate record, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23434140; a copy is included in docs/technical_report/. Contents. Four chains of result directories: casimir/ (Standard Model Casimir weight, gauge and Higgs zero-mode energy, shape Hessian), higgs/ (finite-volume criterion for the Higgs zero mode: Standard Model couplings at the turning-point scale, one-loop finite-volume matching, two-dimensional zero-mode model with cross terms, hazard integral, critical top-quark masses and error budget, real-time ξ_H condition, robustness, universality, two-branch analysis), shape/ (emptiness gate, real-moment theorem, shape fossil, nonlinear survival, Moyal and Wheeler–DeWitt checks, primordial spectra) and cmb/ (temperature and polarization covariance of a three-torus, Fisher information and exact Kullback–Leibler divergences, fossil ensemble, joint inflaton–shape state).
